articles.title: A ‘democratised’ financial crisis is still a crisis
articles.summaryB1:
In recent years, a new type of lending has grown very popular in the United States. It is called private credit, and it means that companies borrow money not from banks, but from private funds. These funds often get their money from insurance companies, which collect premiums from millions of ordinary people. This has made private credit much more widespread than before.

In the past, risky financial activities were mostly limited to large banks and professional investors. Now, however, insurance customers are indirectly connected to these risks, even if they do not know it. If a financial crisis happened, it would no longer affect only wealthy investors. It could also affect regular people who simply bought a life insurance policy.

Regulators are starting to pay attention. They worry that the risks hidden inside private credit funds are not fully visible or well understood. When something goes wrong in finance, the damage can spread quickly to other parts of the economy. This is especially true when many different institutions are connected through shared investments.

The term 'democratised' in the title means that financial risk has spread to more people. But spreading risk does not always make things safer. Sometimes it just means that more people can be hurt when a crisis happens. That is why experts say we need much better oversight of this growing sector.

vocabularyB1.definition: A regular payment made to an insurance company for protection or coverage
Found or happening in many places or among many people
Not in a direct way; through another person, thing, or process
Official supervision or careful watching to make sure rules are followed
A particular area or part of the economy or society

articles.questionB1: If financial risk has become more widespread and now affects ordinary people through insurance, who should be responsible for oversight and protecting them?
articles.summaryB2:
The rapid expansion of private credit in the United States has attracted growing scrutiny, particularly as insurance companies have become one of its principal sources of capital. By channelling policyholders' premiums into private lending funds, insurers have quietly extended the reach of an asset class once confined to sophisticated institutional investors. The result, critics argue, is a form of systemic risk that has been diffused across a far broader population without adequate transparency or informed consent.

Private credit funds typically provide loans to companies that cannot easily access traditional bank financing. These loans are often illiquid and carry higher risk than conventional bonds. When insurance firms allocate their reserves to such instruments, they are effectively exposing millions of retail policyholders to potential losses that those individuals almost certainly do not anticipate.

Proponents of this model argue that it offers attractive returns that help insurers meet their long-term obligations to customers. However, sceptics point out that the opacity of private credit markets makes it extraordinarily difficult for regulators to assess the true scale of embedded risk. Unlike publicly traded securities, private loans are not subject to continuous market pricing, which can mask deteriorating credit quality until problems become acute.

The phrase 'democratised crisis' captures this paradox neatly: spreading access to financial instruments does not inherently reduce vulnerability. If anything, it may simply ensure that when contagion spreads through these interconnected structures, the fallout reaches further than it ever did before.

vocabularyB2.definition: The danger that problems in one part of the financial system will spread and damage the whole economy
Lack of transparency; a situation where information is hidden or difficult to understand
Describing an asset that cannot be quickly or easily sold or converted into cash
The rapid spread of financial problems from one institution or market to others
The negative consequences or damage that follow a harmful event

articles.questionB2: Given the opacity of private credit markets and the risk of contagion, should regulators impose strict limits on how much insurers can invest in illiquid assets, even if this reduces returns for policyholders?

articles.title: Wicker Man director's sons complete their late father's film trilogy
articles.summaryB1: A new film has just been completed, finishing a trilogy of folk horror movies that started more than 50 years ago. The first film in the series was The Wicker Man, made in 1973 by director Robin Hardy. It became a classic of British cinema and is still loved by many fans today. Hardy later made two more films that were meant to be part of the same trilogy, but he died before he could finish the third one. After his death, his sons decided to complete their father's unfinished work. They wanted to bring closure to the story and to their family's long connection with the project. Folk horror is a genre of scary films that uses old traditions, folklore, and rural settings to create fear. The Wicker Man was one of the first films to explore this style, and it influenced many later movies and TV shows. Completing the trilogy was not easy. It took many years of effort and dedication. Hardy's sons felt it was their duty to honour their father's creative vision. For fans of the original film, this final movie offers a chance to see how the saga ends. It is a touching story about family, art, and the desire to finish what you start.

vocabularyB1.definition: A set of three related books, films, or other works that form one story or series.
A feeling that something difficult has ended and you can move forward.
A category or type of art, music, or film with shared features.
Traditional stories, customs, and beliefs passed down through generations in a community.
The quality of working very hard and staying committed to something over a long time.

articles.questionB1: Do you think it is right for a family to complete an unfinished creative project after a loved one dies? What challenges might this dedication involve?
articles.summaryB2: More than half a century after The Wicker Man first unsettled cinema audiences with its blend of paganism, folk ritual, and creeping dread, the trilogy it was intended to launch has finally been brought to completion — not by its original director, but by his sons. Robin Hardy, the filmmaker behind the 1973 cult classic, passed away before he could finalise the third instalment of his folk horror saga. His sons have now stepped in to fulfil that ambition, offering both narrative resolution and a deeply personal sense of legacy for their family. The Wicker Man is widely regarded as a foundational text of folk horror, a subgenre that draws on rural mythology, ancient customs, and communal superstition to generate unease rather than conventional shock tactics. Hardy's subsequent films attempted to expand this eerie, folkloric world, though neither achieved the same critical acclaim or cultural resonance as the original. Completing the trilogy posthumously raises intriguing questions about authorship — specifically, how much of a creative work belongs to its originator and how much can legitimately be shaped by others. Hardy's sons appear to have approached the project as an act of homage rather than reinvention, honouring their father's vision while acknowledging the passage of time. For devotees of folk horror and admirers of the original film alike, the trilogy's completion represents a form of cultural reckoning with an unfinished artistic inheritance.

vocabularyB2.definition: One part of a series of films, books, or other works released separately over time.
Something passed down from a person who has died, such as work, values, or influence.
Happening or appearing after the death of the person responsible for creating it.
The origin of a creative work and the question of who truly created or owns it.
Something done to show deep respect and admiration for a person or their work.

articles.questionB2: When a creative work is completed posthumously by others, how far can authorship genuinely be attributed to the original artist, and does it matter for how we appreciate the final result?

articles.title: Bodies of two hikers missing for decades found after Swiss glacier melts
articles.summaryB1: In 2024, the bodies of two Belgian hikers were discovered in the Swiss Alps. The hikers had gone missing in 1992, more than 30 years ago. Officials believe the bodies were revealed because the Trift Glacier melted and receded over time. A glacier is a large, slow-moving body of ice. When glaciers shrink, they can uncover objects and people that were frozen inside them for many years. The two Belgians were probably hiking in the mountains when they had an accident and died. Their bodies were then covered by ice and snow. Because the glacier has been melting due to rising temperatures, the ice slowly disappeared and the remains were finally found. This discovery is both sad for the victims' families and a powerful reminder of how climate change affects our world. Scientists say that glaciers around the world are retreating faster than before. As ice melts, more lost items, animals, and even human remains are being uncovered. This shows that the environment is changing in ways that have real and personal consequences for people. The story also highlights how long families sometimes have to wait for answers about missing loved ones.

vocabularyB1.definition: To move back or become smaller, especially water or ice
The body of a dead person or animal found after death
To find something hidden, or to remove what was covering it
Moving back or becoming smaller over time
Results or effects that happen because of an action or event

articles.questionB1: What consequences do you think it has for families and communities when missing people are finally found after many years?
articles.summaryB2: Swiss authorities have confirmed the discovery of the remains of two Belgian nationals who vanished in the Alps in 1992, more than three decades after they were reported missing. The bodies were found after the Trift Glacier receded substantially, exposing what the ice had long concealed. While the identities of the victims have not been publicly disclosed in detail, officials have confirmed their Belgian origin and linked the discovery directly to glacial retreat driven by rising temperatures. The case is a sobering illustration of how accelerating climate change is reshaping Alpine terrain in ways that extend well beyond environmental statistics. As glaciers across Switzerland and the broader Alpine region continue to shrink at an alarming rate, they are progressively yielding long-frozen secrets — from ancient artefacts to the bodies of climbers and hikers who met their fate on the ice decades ago. This phenomenon, sometimes referred to as glacial archaeology, has grown more frequent in recent years as melt seasons intensify. For the families of the two Belgians, the discovery may bring a measure of closure after decades of uncertainty. However, the circumstances also prompt reflection on the sheer pace of glacial loss and what it signals about the health of mountain ecosystems. Scientists warn that without dramatic reductions in global emissions, Switzerland could lose the majority of its glaciers by the end of this century.

vocabularyB2.definition: The process by which a glacier shrinks and moves back due to melting
Hidden from view; kept out of sight
A feeling of resolution or peace after a difficult or uncertain situation
Making you think seriously about something; removing false optimism
Producing or giving something up, often gradually or reluctantly

articles.questionB2: To what extent does the discovery of human remains through glacial retreat force us to reconsider the true human cost of climate change beyond abstract statistics and yielding environmental data?

articles.title: Twelve killed as Polish coach crashes in Hungary
articles.summaryB1:
On 16 August 2026, a coach carrying Catholic pilgrims crashed in Hungary, killing twelve people. The bus was travelling back to Poland after what is believed to have been a religious journey. The accident happened on a Hungarian road and caused shock in both Poland and Hungary.

Catholic pilgrimages are a strong tradition in Poland. Every year, thousands of Polish believers travel to holy sites in Poland and abroad. Groups often travel together by coach, which makes accidents like this especially tragic because so many people are affected at once.

The crash killed twelve passengers and is likely to have injured others, though the exact number of casualties was not immediately confirmed. Emergency services arrived at the scene to help survivors and recover the victims.

This disaster has drawn attention to the safety of long-distance coach travel in Europe. Many pilgrim groups are made up of elderly people who rely on buses to make these journeys. When a vehicle carrying so many passengers is involved in a serious accident, the loss of life can be devastating.

Polish authorities have expressed grief over the tragedy and are cooperating with Hungarian officials to investigate the cause of the crash. The families of the victims are waiting for more information about what exactly happened on that road in Hungary.

vocabularyB1.definition: People who travel to a holy or religious place as an act of faith
People who are killed or injured in an accident or disaster
A large comfortable bus used for long-distance travel
Causing great shock, sadness, or destruction
Working together with someone to achieve something

articles.questionB1: Why do you think coach travel can be especially devastating when an accident happens, and how could pilgrim groups stay safer on long journeys?
articles.summaryB2:
A coach carrying Catholic pilgrims back to Poland crashed in Hungary on 16 August 2026, killing twelve people in one of the deadliest road accidents involving Polish nationals in recent memory. The bus, which had been on a religious journey, came to grief on a Hungarian road, prompting an immediate response from emergency services and triggering expressions of mourning from officials on both sides of the border.

Pilgrimage holds deep cultural and spiritual significance in Poland, where organised group travel to sacred sites remains a widespread practice. Coaches are the predominant mode of transport for such groups, particularly among older believers for whom air or rail travel may be less accessible. This reliance on road transport exposes participants to the inherent risks of long-distance travel, risks that this tragedy has thrown into sharp relief.

The incident has reignited debate about the safety standards applied to coaches operating across European borders. Questions are likely to arise about vehicle maintenance, driver fatigue, and whether existing EU regulations are consistently enforced on routes that span multiple countries.

Polish authorities have pledged to liaise with their Hungarian counterparts to establish the precise circumstances of the crash. For the bereaved families waiting anxiously for news, however, procedural investigations offer little comfort. The accident serves as a sombre reminder of the fragility of life and the profound grief that mass-casualty events inflict on tight-knit communities.

vocabularyB2.definition: Started again, especially a debate or feeling that had stopped for a while
Deeply saddened by the death of a loved one; in a state of grief after loss
To communicate and work closely with another person or organisation
Serious, sad, and without brightness or cheerfulness
Existing as a natural and permanent part of something

articles.questionB2: To what extent do you think existing EU regulations are sufficient to address the inherent safety risks of long-distance coach travel, and who should bear responsibility when such tragedies occur?

articles.title: Europe’s dry rivers are exposing mammoths and Nazi warships
articles.summaryB1: Europe is experiencing record heat and severe drought this summer. As a result, many rivers across the continent have very low water levels. This is a problem for people, agriculture, and wildlife. However, the dry conditions are also revealing surprising things that were hidden underwater for many years. In some rivers, scientists have discovered the bones of woolly mammoths, ancient animals that lived thousands of years ago. These discoveries help researchers learn more about prehistoric life in Europe. In other parts of the continent, the low water is exposing old shipwrecks from the Second World War. Some of these are German military vessels that sank decades ago. Locals and tourists are visiting these unusual sights along dried-out riverbanks. Experts warn that the drought is connected to climate change, which is making extreme weather more common in Europe. The summers are getting hotter and drier, putting stress on water supplies and ecosystems. While the unexpected discoveries are fascinating, they are a reminder that something is seriously wrong with the environment. Governments and scientists are calling for stronger action to reduce carbon emissions and protect rivers. The situation shows how climate change can have both dramatic and unexpected effects on the world around us.

vocabularyB1.definition: A long period of time with very little or no rain, causing water shortages
Showing something that was previously hidden or not known
Relating to the time in history before anything was written down
Destroyed or sunken ships, usually found at the bottom of water
Gases or other substances released into the air, especially from burning fuel

articles.questionB1: The drought is revealing hidden objects from the past — do you think such discoveries change the way people think about climate change and protecting the environment?
articles.summaryB2: A prolonged and record-breaking drought gripping much of Europe this summer has caused river levels to plummet to historic lows, exposing an extraordinary array of submerged relics. While the human and ecological toll of the dry spell is severe — straining water supplies, disrupting agriculture, and threatening aquatic biodiversity — the receding waters have also uncovered unexpected archaeological and historical treasures. Among the most striking finds are the skeletal remains of woolly mammoths, unearthed from riverbeds where they had lain undisturbed for millennia. These specimens are providing palaeontologists with rare insights into the distribution and behaviour of megafauna in prehistoric Europe. Simultaneously, the low waters have laid bare the rusting hulks of warships from the Second World War, including Nazi German military vessels that sank in European rivers during the conflict. These ghostly remnants are drawing curious visitors to riverbanks that would normally be deep underwater. Scientists are unequivocal in linking the severity of the drought to accelerating climate change, which is intensifying the frequency and magnitude of extreme weather events across the continent. While the unearthed discoveries capture public imagination, researchers caution that they are symptomatic of a deeply troubling environmental trajectory. European policymakers face mounting pressure to implement ambitious decarbonisation strategies and invest in water resilience, as the gap between climate commitments and real-world outcomes grows ever more apparent.

vocabularyB2.definition: To fall or drop very quickly and steeply to a much lower level
Objects or remains that have survived from an earlier time in history
Scientists who study ancient life through the examination of fossils and bones
Completely clear and leaving no doubt or possibility of misunderstanding
The process of reducing or eliminating carbon dioxide emissions from an economy or system

articles.questionB2: Given that the unearthed relics are simultaneously scientifically valuable and symptomatic of environmental crisis, how should governments and the media balance public fascination with the urgency of the underlying climate emergency?

articles.title: Europe’s biggest Virgin Mary statue – taller than Rio’s Christ the Redeemer – unveiled in Polish village
articles.summaryB1: A giant statue of the Virgin Mary has been unveiled in a small village in Poland. The statue is 55.6 metres tall, which makes it the biggest statue of the Virgin Mary in Europe. It is even taller than the famous Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, which stands at about 38 metres. The Polish statue towers over the surrounding countryside, and people can see it from many kilometres away. The monument was paid for by a local couple who have a lot of money. They wanted to do something special for their community and for their Catholic faith. Poland is a deeply religious country, and the Catholic Church plays a big role in everyday life there. Many Poles feel a strong connection to the Virgin Mary, who is sometimes called the Queen of Poland. Large religious monuments are not unusual in Poland. For example, a giant statue of Jesus Christ was built in the town of Świebodzin in 2010. The new statue has attracted a lot of attention both inside and outside Poland. Some people admire the dedication of the couple who funded it. Others wonder whether such a large monument was the best way to spend that money. The statue was unveiled on 15 August, which is a national holiday in Poland celebrating the Virgin Mary.

vocabularyB1.definition: Officially shown to the public for the first time
A large structure built to remember a person or event
Is much taller than everything around it
Paid for something, usually a large or public project
Strong belief in a religion or in God

articles.questionB1: The monument was funded by a wealthy couple. Do you think private individuals should pay for large religious structures in public spaces? Why?
articles.summaryB2:
Poland has unveiled what is now Europe's tallest statue of the Virgin Mary, a towering 55.6-metre monument erected in a rural village and funded entirely by a wealthy local couple. The structure surpasses the globally renowned Christ the Redeemer in Rio de Janeiro, which stands at roughly 38 metres, immediately drawing international media attention and sparking debate about the role of private patronage in shaping public religious spaces.

Poland has long maintained a deep and visible devotion to Marian tradition — the Virgin Mary holds a quasi-national status, widely referred to as the Queen of Poland — and large-scale religious monuments are not without precedent. The Jesus Christ statue in Świebodzin, completed in 2010, similarly captured global headlines and stirred controversy at home.

The new statue was unveiled on 15 August, the Feast of the Assumption, a public holiday in Poland that carries both religious and historical resonance, commemorating the 1920 Battle of Warsaw as well as Marian devotion.

Reactions have been mixed. Supporters view the monument as a bold expression of collective piety and a potential draw for religious tourism. Critics, however, question whether the expenditure reflects sound priorities, particularly in a rural area where public infrastructure may be underfunded. The fact that it was privately commissioned rather than state-funded adds another layer to the discussion, raising questions about how personal wealth intersects with communal identity and shared public space.

vocabularyB2.definition: Financial support given by a wealthy person to fund a project or cause
An earlier example that makes a later similar action seem normal or acceptable
The quality of having deep meaning or emotional importance for many people
Strong religious devotion and respect for one's faith
Officially ordered and paid for a piece of work, such as a building or statue

articles.questionB2: Given that the statue was privately commissioned rather than state-funded, to what extent should personal patronage determine what becomes a permanent feature of a community's shared public space?

articles.title: Poland hit by theft of 19 million patients’ data from medical platform
articles.summaryB1:
In August 2025, Poland experienced a major data breach. Hackers stole personal information belonging to about 19 million patients from a medical platform. This is one of the largest incidents of its kind in Poland's history. The digital affairs minister made this statement publicly, showing how serious the situation is.

The stolen data came from a platform that stores medical records. This kind of platform collects sensitive information, such as names, addresses, and health details. When this information falls into the wrong hands, it can be used for fraud or blackmail.

Data breaches like this are a growing problem across Europe. Many countries are working to protect their citizens' personal information. In Poland, this incident has shocked many people because of how large it is. Nineteen million records is a very high number — it represents almost half of Poland's total population.

The authorities are now investigating how the breach happened. They want to find out if the platform had enough security measures in place. Patients who may have been affected are being advised to stay alert for any suspicious activity related to their personal details.

This event reminds us how important it is to keep our data safe online. Both governments and private companies must take steps to protect the information they store on behalf of ordinary people.

vocabularyB1.definition: When private information is stolen or accessed by someone without permission
Private and personal; information that could cause harm if shared publicly
Dishonest activity done to trick people and steal money or advantages
Official organisations or people, such as the police or government, with power to act
Making you feel that something is wrong or dishonest

articles.questionB1: After a data breach like this, what should ordinary people do to protect their sensitive personal information?
articles.summaryB2:
Poland has suffered what officials are describing as one of the gravest cybersecurity incidents in the country's history, after hackers successfully exfiltrated personal data belonging to approximately 19 million patients from a medical platform. The scale of the theft is staggering: 19 million records represents nearly half of Poland's entire population, meaning the potential for widespread harm is enormous.

The digital affairs minister went on record to characterise the breach as one of the largest of its kind ever recorded in Poland, a statement that reflects both the severity of the attack and the vulnerability of health data infrastructure to malicious actors. Medical platforms typically hold some of the most confidential information individuals possess — including diagnoses, prescriptions, and contact details — making such records particularly attractive targets for cybercriminals seeking to exploit them for identity theft, extortion, or sale on illicit markets.

The incident comes amid growing scrutiny of how healthcare providers and digital health platforms across Europe safeguard patient data. Under GDPR regulations, organisations that fail to adequately protect personal information face substantial financial penalties, and affected individuals are legally entitled to be notified of risks to their data.

Investigations are now under way to establish how the perpetrators gained access and whether adequate safeguards were in place prior to the attack. This case will almost certainly intensify pressure on both public institutions and private operators to reassess their cybersecurity protocols and invest more heavily in digital defences.

vocabularyB2.definition: Secretly removed or stolen data from a system without authorisation
A weakness that makes something or someone open to attack or damage
Very careful and detailed examination or attention by others
People who carry out a harmful, illegal, or criminal act
Official sets of rules or procedures followed in a particular situation

articles.questionB2: Given the vulnerability of health data systems exposed by this breach, what responsibilities do governments and private operators share in protecting citizens' medical information, and how should perpetrators be held accountable?

articles.title: How—and how much—should central banks talk?
articles.summaryB1: Central banks are powerful institutions that control interest rates and money supply in a country. In recent years, they have started to communicate much more with the public. They give speeches, publish reports, and hold press conferences regularly. But is this a good thing? The question is how much central banks should talk and what they should say. When a central bank speaks clearly, people and businesses can make better financial decisions. For example, if a bank signals that interest rates will rise, companies can plan ahead. However, too much communication can cause problems. If bank officials send mixed messages, it can confuse investors and create uncertainty in financial markets. There is also the risk that central banks promise things they cannot deliver. This damages their credibility, which is the trust that people place in them. Experts argue that the best approach is balance. A central bank should explain its decisions and give guidance about the future, but it should not say too much or make promises that are too specific. The article compares this to an art form — saying enough to be helpful, but not so much that it creates new problems. For Polish savers and businesses, this matters because decisions made by major central banks affect interest rates and economic conditions across Europe and the world.

vocabularyB1.definition: The percentage charged for borrowing money or earned on savings.
The quality of being trusted and believed by other people.
A situation where you do not know what will happen in the future.
Information or advice that helps people make decisions or plan ahead.
To give a hint or indirect message about future plans or actions.

articles.questionB1: How much guidance do you think central banks should give to the public about future interest rates, and why?
articles.summaryB2: Central banks have undergone a dramatic transformation in how they communicate with the outside world. Once famously secretive — the former Federal Reserve chair Alan Greenspan was said to pride himself on deliberate obscurity — these institutions now flood markets with speeches, forward guidance, and detailed policy statements. The question is whether this torrent of communication has gone too far. The core argument is that transparency, while broadly desirable, carries diminishing returns. When central banks articulate their intentions clearly, businesses, investors, and households can make well-informed decisions, reducing volatility in financial markets. Forward guidance — the practice of signalling future policy moves — became especially popular after the 2008 financial crisis, when interest rates hit zero and central banks needed new tools to steer expectations. Yet the pitfalls of over-communication are equally real. Officials who speak too frequently or with excessive specificity can inadvertently box themselves in, leaving little room for pragmatic adjustment when economic conditions shift unexpectedly. Conflicting statements from different bank officials can also erode market confidence, sending contradictory signals that amplify rather than calm investor anxiety. There is also a deeper accountability problem: the more central banks promise, the more exposed they become when those promises prove untenable. The article frames the challenge as an art — calibrating the volume and precision of communication to maximise clarity without sacrificing the institutional flexibility that sound policymaking demands. For economies integrated into global capital flows, the stakes of getting this balance wrong are considerable.

vocabularyB2.definition: Official statements from a central bank about its likely future policy decisions.
Frequent and unpredictable changes in prices or values in financial markets.
Without intending to; accidentally doing something as an unplanned side effect.
Impossible to defend or maintain; no longer able to be supported or justified.
Carefully adjusting something to achieve exactly the right level or balance.

articles.questionB2: Given the risks of over-promising, how should central banks balance the need for forward guidance with the flexibility required to respond to rapidly changing economic conditions?

articles.title: Trump envoy Kushner arrives in Israel after rare Hamas talks on Gaza peace plan
articles.summaryB1:
Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, has travelled to Israel to meet Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The visit comes after Kushner held rare talks with Hamas, the group that controls the Gaza Strip. These discussions are part of an effort to find a peace plan for the region.

The conflict in Gaza began in October 2023, when Hamas attacked Israel. Since then, the fighting has caused enormous suffering for people living in Gaza. Many countries and international organisations have been trying to negotiate a ceasefire, which means an agreement to stop the fighting.

Kushner played a major role in Middle East diplomacy during Trump's first time as president. He helped create the Abraham Accords, a set of agreements between Israel and several Arab countries. Now, with Trump back in the White House, Kushner has returned to the region as an envoy, which is a person sent by a government to represent it in talks with other countries or groups.

The fact that Kushner met with Hamas before arriving in Israel is considered unusual. Hamas is regarded as a terrorist organisation by the United States and several other countries. Many people are watching these talks closely, hoping that they might lead to a ceasefire and the release of hostages still held in Gaza.

vocabularyB1.definition: An agreement between two sides in a conflict to stop fighting for a period of time
A person officially sent by a government to represent it in talks or negotiations
To discuss something formally in order to reach an agreement between two or more sides
People held prisoner by a group, often to be exchanged for something the group wants
Something that does not happen very often and is therefore unusual or surprising

articles.questionB1: Why do you think it is rare for a US envoy to negotiate directly with a group like Hamas, and what difficulties might this cause?
articles.summaryB2:
Jared Kushner, serving as an informal envoy for his father-in-law President Donald Trump, arrived in Israel on Monday for a scheduled meeting with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The visit follows a striking development: Kushner had already held direct talks with Hamas, the Palestinian militant group that governs the Gaza Strip — a move that signals a potentially unconventional approach to resolving one of the world's most entrenched conflicts.

Hamas is designated a terrorist organisation by the United States, the European Union, and several other governments, making high-level American contact with the group highly contentious. Critics argue that engaging directly with Hamas risks legitimising the organisation, while proponents suggest that any realistic path to a ceasefire and the release of hostages must involve talking to the parties who actually hold power on the ground.

Kushner was a central architect of Middle East policy during Trump's first administration, most notably brokering the Abraham Accords — a series of normalisation agreements between Israel and Arab states including the UAE and Bahrain. His re-emergence on the diplomatic stage suggests that the Trump administration intends to pursue its own distinct framework for resolving the Gaza conflict, potentially bypassing traditional multilateral channels.

The outcome of Kushner's talks with Netanyahu remains to be seen, but the sequence of events — Hamas first, Israel second — has already drawn considerable attention from analysts and diplomats watching the region closely.

vocabularyB2.definition: Deeply established and very difficult to change, often referring to conflicts or attitudes
Causing strong disagreement or argument among people with opposing views
Making something appear acceptable, legal, or officially recognised by treating it seriously
Arranging or negotiating a deal or agreement between two or more parties
Involving three or more countries or groups working together on a shared issue

articles.questionB2: To what extent does Kushner's decision to meet Hamas before Netanyahu suggest a deliberate shift in US strategy, and could legitimising such contact ultimately help or hinder prospects for a lasting ceasefire?

articles.title: Ebola outbreak in DR Congo becomes deadliest in its history
articles.summaryB1: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is facing its deadliest Ebola outbreak ever recorded. Ebola is a serious disease that spreads through contact with the blood or body fluids of infected people. This current outbreak has killed more people than any previous one in the country's history, making it a major health emergency. What makes this situation especially alarming is that it is also the fastest growing outbreak on record. The disease spreading now is caused by a rare species of Ebola called Bundibugyo, which is not the most common type. The DRC has suffered many Ebola outbreaks before, so health workers there have experience dealing with this disease. However, the speed and scale of this outbreak are putting enormous pressure on the healthcare system. International health organisations are working to contain the spread and treat those who are infected. People living in affected areas are being warned to avoid contact with sick individuals and to seek medical help quickly if they feel unwell. The situation is being closely monitored by the World Health Organisation. Outbreaks like this one remind us how quickly a dangerous disease can spread and why strong public health systems matter so much for communities around the world.

vocabularyB1.definition: A sudden start or increase of a disease affecting many people in one area.
Causing worry or fear because something seems dangerous or serious.
Not common; something that does not happen or exist very often.
To stop something from spreading or getting bigger.
Changed or harmed by something, such as a disease or disaster.

articles.questionB1: Why do you think it is so difficult to contain an outbreak of a dangerous disease like Ebola in some parts of the world?
articles.summaryB2: The Democratic Republic of Congo is grappling with the deadliest Ebola outbreak in its history, a grim milestone that has sent shockwaves through the global health community. The current crisis, driven by the Bundibugyo strain — a rare and less frequently studied species of the Ebola virus — has also been classified as the fastest growing outbreak on record, compounding fears about the country's capacity to mount an effective response. The DRC has long been considered one of the most Ebola-prone nations in the world, having endured multiple outbreaks over several decades. Despite this accumulated experience, the sheer velocity of the current surge is overwhelming already strained health infrastructure. Aid agencies and international bodies, including the World Health Organisation, are mobilising resources to support containment efforts, though logistical challenges in remote regions continue to hamper progress. The Bundibugyo strain was first identified in Uganda in 2007 and is associated with lower fatality rates than the more notorious Zaire strain, yet its rapid proliferation in this instance has prompted urgent concern among epidemiologists. The outbreak also exposes persistent vulnerabilities in public health systems across conflict-affected regions, where access to medical care remains severely restricted. As the death toll mounts, the international community faces renewed pressure to address the structural inequalities that allow such epidemics to take hold and escalate unchecked.

vocabularyB2.definition: Struggling to deal with a difficult or complex problem or situation.
Making an already bad or difficult situation worse by adding more problems.
A rapid increase or spread of something, especially something harmful.
Scientists who study how diseases spread through populations and how to control them.
Weaknesses that make a person, system, or place likely to be harmed or damaged.

articles.questionB2: To what extent do the structural vulnerabilities exposed by this outbreak reflect failures of international health policy, and what systemic changes might prevent such rapid proliferation of disease in conflict-affected regions?

articles.title: Four 'extraordinary' Renaissance paintings stolen from Italian museum
articles.summaryB1: Four paintings from the Renaissance period have been stolen from a museum in Italy. The theft happened at night, and the thieves managed to take the works without triggering any alarms. Because of this, police believe the robbery was carefully planned by professionals. The paintings are described as 'extraordinary' and are considered very valuable, both artistically and historically. Renaissance art was created in Europe between roughly the 14th and 17th centuries and is highly prized around the world. Museums in Italy hold some of the finest collections of this type of art. When a theft like this occurs without any alarms going off, it often suggests that the criminals had inside knowledge or specialist equipment. Investigators are now trying to find out who took the paintings and where they might be. Art theft is a serious crime because stolen works are often hidden for many years and may never be recovered. Italy has experienced art thefts before, and the authorities have dedicated teams that deal with these crimes. Cases like this remind us how difficult it can be to protect cultural treasures, even in secure buildings. The public and the art world are watching closely, hoping the paintings will be found and returned safely.

vocabularyB1.definition: The act of stealing something from a person or place.
To cause something to start or happen, for example an alarm.
Considered very valuable or special by people.
Found and returned after being lost or stolen.
Very valuable objects, often with cultural or historical importance.

articles.questionB1: Why do you think some stolen treasures are never recovered, even when police investigate the theft for many years?
articles.summaryB2: Four Renaissance paintings, described by officials as 'extraordinary', have been taken from an Italian museum in what investigators suspect was a meticulously orchestrated professional heist. The thieves carried out the operation overnight, managing to bypass the building's security systems entirely without triggering a single alarm — a detail that has fuelled suspicion of highly trained perpetrators with possible insider knowledge or access to sophisticated equipment. Renaissance works, produced during one of Europe's most celebrated cultural and artistic periods, command enormous sums on the black market precisely because they are so rarely available through legitimate channels. Italy, home to an unrivalled concentration of such masterpieces, has long been a target for organised art crime. The country's Carabinieri TPC — a specialist unit dedicated to protecting cultural heritage — is expected to lead the investigation. Art stolen in professional heists of this kind frequently disappears into private collections or is used as collateral in criminal negotiations, making recovery exceptionally difficult. The incident has reignited debate about the adequacy of security measures in smaller regional museums, which often lack the resources to match the protection afforded to larger, more prominent institutions. For the art world, the loss of even a single Renaissance work represents an irreplaceable gap in the shared cultural record — four such pieces disappearing simultaneously is, by any measure, a deeply troubling development.

articles.title: Spanish nanomaterial cools surfaces by 12.9°C without electricity
articles.summaryB1:
Scientists in Spain have created a special material that can cool buildings, cars, and electronic devices without using any electricity. The material was developed by researchers at CSIC, a large scientific organisation in Spain.

The material is made from a polymer, which is a type of substance built from long chains of molecules. It works by releasing heat upward into space rather than letting it stay trapped near a surface. The energy used to do this comes from sunlight, so no power source is needed.

In tests, the material was able to reduce surface temperatures by up to 12.9 degrees Celsius. This is a remarkable result because it happens passively, meaning the material does not need a machine or engine to work.

This technology could be very useful in hot countries or during summer heatwaves. Air conditioning systems use a lot of electricity and produce greenhouse gases, so finding alternatives is a priority for scientists and governments. A material that can dissipate heat naturally could help reduce energy bills and lower carbon emissions.

The researchers believe this nanostructure could be applied to rooftops, vehicle surfaces, and electronic equipment. If the technology moves from the laboratory to real-world use, it could make a genuine difference to how we cool our homes and reduce our dependence on traditional air conditioning systems.

vocabularyB1.definition: A material made from long chains of molecules, used in plastics and many other products
Working automatically without needing extra energy, effort, or a machine to operate
To spread and release something, like heat, so it disappears or moves away

articles.questionB1: Do you think materials that passively cool buildings could reduce our dependence on air conditioning in Polish summers? Why or why not?
articles.summaryB2:
A team of researchers at Spain's CSIC institute has developed a polymer nanostructure capable of lowering surface temperatures by up to 12.9 degrees Celsius without consuming any electricity. The technology works through a process called radiative cooling, in which the material dissipates thermal energy directly into outer space by exploiting solar radiation. Because it operates entirely passively, it requires no mechanical systems, making it a potentially low-cost and low-maintenance solution for thermal management.

The implications of this breakthrough are far-reaching. Conventional air conditioning accounts for a substantial and growing share of global electricity consumption, and its widespread use contributes to urban heat islands as well as greenhouse gas emissions. A material that can mitigate surface heat without drawing on the power grid could ease pressure on energy infrastructure, particularly during peak summer demand.

The researchers envision applications across several sectors, including architecture, the automotive industry, and consumer electronics. Coating rooftops or vehicle exteriors with such a nanostructure could reduce the need for active cooling systems, thereby cutting both energy costs and carbon footprints.

Critics may question whether the material can maintain its efficacy under real-world conditions such as dust accumulation, humidity, or prolonged exposure to ultraviolet radiation. Scaling up production from laboratory samples to commercially viable quantities also remains a challenge. Nevertheless, the CSIC findings represent a noteworthy step toward sustainable, electricity-free cooling at a time when demand for innovative thermal solutions continues to grow.

articles.questionB2: Given the questions surrounding the long-term efficacy of new materials under real-world conditions, how realistic is it to expect radiative cooling technology to replace conventional air conditioning at scale?

articles.title: Portugal is home to hundreds of ancient olive trees, one may be over 3,700 years old
articles.summaryB1:
Portugal is home to hundreds of very old olive trees, and scientists are now working to find out exactly how old they are. A team from the University of Trás-os-Montes and Alto Douro, known as UTAD, has developed a scientific method to date these ancient trees. Their work is taking place across the whole country.

One of the most exciting discoveries is in a town called Vidigueira. Scientists believe that an olive tree there may be over 3,700 years old. If this is correct, the tree was already alive during the Bronze Age, long before many modern civilisations existed.

Olive trees are common in Portugal and are part of everyday life and culture. However, most people did not realise that some of these trees could be so ancient. The new method allows researchers to estimate the age of a tree more accurately than before.

This discovery matters for several reasons. Ancient trees are a natural heritage that connects us to the distant past. They also provide useful information about climate and the environment over thousands of years. Protecting these trees means preserving something rare and valuable.

The research shows that Portugal may have some of the oldest living olive trees in the world. Scientists hope that their method will help identify and protect more of these remarkable trees in the future.

vocabularyB1.definition: Very old, existing for thousands of years
A planned way of doing something to achieve a result
To calculate an approximate number or amount, not exact

articles.questionB1: Why do you think it is valuable to protect ancient trees that are part of a country's natural heritage?
articles.summaryB2:
Portugal has long been associated with olive cultivation, but a groundbreaking scientific initiative is now revealing just how extraordinary the country's olive trees truly are. A research team from the University of Trás-os-Montes and Alto Douro has devised a dating methodology capable of determining the age of ancient olive trees with greater precision than conventional techniques. The project spans hundreds of trees across the country.

The most striking finding so far concerns a tree in Vidigueira, which researchers believe may be over 3,700 years old. If verified, this would place the tree's origins in the Bronze Age, predating many of the world's great ancient civilisations. Such a lifespan is extraordinary even by the standards of long-lived species, and the discovery has attracted considerable attention from the scientific community.

Beyond the appeal of record-breaking ages, the research carries real ecological and historical weight. Ancient olive trees serve as living archives, potentially encoding within their rings and tissues data about past climates, droughts and human land use stretching back millennia. This makes them invaluable to environmental scientists and historians alike.

The project also prompts a conversation about conservation priorities. Portugal's ancient trees are largely unprotected, and many face threats from agricultural intensification and development. Establishing their age through rigorous scientific scrutiny could provide the evidence needed to advocate for stronger legal protection.

Ultimately, this research positions Portugal as a custodian of some of the world's oldest living organisms, reframing its ancient olive groves as irreplaceable natural monuments.

articles.title: ‘I’ve never done anything like this in my life’: Marina Abramović on making art with balloons
articles.summaryB1:
Marina Abramović is a famous performance artist known for creating unusual and sometimes challenging art experiences. Her latest work is very different from anything she has done before. She has created an installation called 'Snowy/Windy/Spring on Planet Z' at the Balloon Museum in New York. This is described as the first permanent museum dedicated to inflatable art.

Visitors walk through a glowing white room filled with oversized inflatable blades of grass that touch their faces. Small paper squares that look like snow blow through the air. The path curves, so you cannot see very far ahead, and the journey feels longer than expected.

Abramović admitted that when she first received the assignment, she thought balloon art was 'kitschy' – meaning cheap and designed mainly for children. However, she began to contemplate the deeper meaning of balloons. She noticed a connection between balloons and her own art practice. A balloon is filled with air, and at some point that air disappears. This idea of something temporary and alive connects directly to her work.

The Balloon Museum recently opened in New York and gives inflatable art a permanent home. Abramović spoke about the project from her Manhattan apartment. Her willingness to explore a completely new type of art shows how creative artists can find inspiration in unexpected places.

vocabularyB1.definition: A type of artwork that fills a space and which visitors can walk through or experience.

articles.questionB1: Abramović accepted this assignment even though she found balloon art 'kitschy' at first. Can you think of a time when you changed your opinion about something after contemplating it more carefully?
articles.summaryB2:
Marina Abramović, the Serbian-born performance artist celebrated for decades of boundary-pushing work involving endurance and the human body, has taken a striking creative detour into the world of inflatable art. Her new installation, 'Snowy/Windy/Spring on Planet Z', is now on display at the Balloon Museum in New York – an institution that bills itself as the first permanent home dedicated exclusively to inflatable art.

The experience is deliberately disorienting. Visitors wind through a luminous white space where oversized inflatable blades of grass brush against their faces and paper snow swirls through the air. The curving path obscures what lies ahead, creating an uncanny sense that the journey stretches far beyond the room's actual dimensions.

Speaking via Zoom from her Manhattan apartment, Abramović described the project as unlike anything she had previously attempted. Her initial reaction to balloon art was one of scepticism – she dismissed it as kitschy and superficial, essentially the domain of children's entertainment. Yet the more she reflected on the medium, the more she discerned unexpected resonance with her longstanding artistic concerns. A balloon, she observed, is animated by air and ultimately defined by its own ephemerality – a quality central to performance art itself.

This willingness to engage with an ostensibly lowbrow medium and find within it genuine conceptual depth is characteristic of Abramović's career. The collaboration also signals how institutions like the Balloon Museum are striving to position inflatable art as a serious cultural form worthy of critical attention.

articles.title: Donald Trump’s Arctic threats are pushing Iceland towards Europe
articles.summaryB1: Iceland is a small island country in the North Atlantic Ocean. It is not a member of the European Union. But now, Icelanders are voting on whether to start talking about joining the EU again. Why is this happening? One big reason is US President Donald Trump. Trump has made threats about the Arctic region, which includes areas near Iceland. This has made many Icelanders feel worried about their country's safety and future. Iceland already has strong ties to Europe through trade and geography. However, it has stayed outside the EU for many years. Some Icelanders want to keep their independence, especially regarding fishing rights, which are very valuable to their economy. Others feel that joining the EU would give Iceland more protection and a stronger voice in the world. Trump's aggressive statements about the Arctic have changed the political debate in Iceland. More people now support the idea of membership talks than before. The vote does not mean Iceland will definitely join the EU. It only decides whether official talks should begin again. These talks stopped years ago. The situation shows how actions by powerful countries, like the United States, can push smaller nations to reconsider their alliances and look for new forms of security and cooperation.

articles.questionB1: Do you think small countries should reconsider their alliances when powerful nations make threats? What would you do in Iceland's position?
articles.summaryB2: Iceland, a strategically located island in the North Atlantic that has long maintained an ambivalent relationship with European integration, is now holding a referendum on whether to reopen accession talks with the European Union. The vote has been largely catalysed by Donald Trump's increasingly assertive posture towards the Arctic, a region where Iceland holds considerable geopolitical exposure. Trump's rhetoric about Arctic dominance has unsettled Icelanders who previously felt relatively insulated from great-power rivalry, prompting a reassessment of the country's security arrangements. Iceland applied for EU membership in 2009 but suspended negotiations in 2015, primarily due to domestic opposition centred on fishing rights — a sector that underpins the national economy and carries deep cultural resonance. The prospect of surrendering control over Icelandic waters to EU common fisheries policy has historically been a dealbreaker for many voters. However, Trump's belligerent Arctic declarations appear to have shifted the calculus for a portion of the electorate, making EU membership look less like an economic concession and more like a geopolitical safeguard. The referendum does not commit Iceland to joining the EU; it merely determines whether formal accession negotiations should resume. Nevertheless, the vote reflects a broader recalibration of how small, exposed nations weigh sovereignty against collective security in an era of resurgent great-power competition. The outcome could have ripple effects across other non-EU European states watching closely.

articles.title: Ancient Roman shipwreck discovered off Sicily coast
articles.summaryB1:
Divers have discovered an ancient Roman shipwreck near the coast of Sicily, an island in southern Italy. The wreck is believed to be around 2,000 years old, dating back to the time of the Roman Empire. It was found on the seabed at a depth of about 80 metres, which helped to preserve it well over the centuries.

The ship was carrying a large cargo of amphorae, which are tall clay containers that the Romans used to transport goods such as wine, olive oil, and fish sauce. Many of these containers were found intact, still sitting in neat rows inside the wreck. Experts say this gives them a rare chance to study how Roman trade worked across the Mediterranean Sea.

Italy's culture minister described the find as one of the most remarkable underwater archaeological discoveries in recent years. Archaeologists are now working carefully to document and protect the site before any objects are removed.

This discovery matters because it adds to our understanding of ancient Roman life and commerce. Sicily was a very active region for trade in Roman times, and wrecks like this one help historians piece together how goods and ideas moved between different parts of the empire. It is a reminder that the sea still holds many secrets from the past.

articles.questionB1: Why do you think discoveries like this shipwreck are valuable for our understanding of ancient commerce and everyday life?
articles.summaryB2:
Underwater archaeologists have unearthed a remarkably well-preserved Roman shipwreck off the coast of Sicily, in what Italy's culture minister has hailed as one of the most exceptional submarine archaeological finds in recent memory. The vessel, estimated to be approximately 2,000 years old, was located on the seabed at a depth of roughly 80 metres — a depth sufficient to shield it from the wave action and human interference that typically accelerates deterioration closer to the surface.

Among the most striking aspects of the discovery is the shipwreck's cargo: rows of amphorae, the distinctive elongated clay vessels used throughout the Roman world to transport commodities including wine, olive oil, and garum, a fermented fish sauce prized across the empire. A number of these containers reportedly remain intact, offering archaeologists an extraordinary window into Roman maritime trade networks and the logistics of long-distance commerce in the ancient Mediterranean.

The find carries considerable weight for historians studying Roman economic history, as physical evidence of this calibre is rare. Sicily occupied a strategic position within the empire's trade routes, serving as a conduit between the eastern and western Mediterranean, and wrecks of this kind can help scholars reconstruct the volume, variety, and direction of goods in circulation.

Authorities have indicated that a thorough documentation process will precede any retrieval of artefacts, ensuring the site's integrity is maintained throughout the investigation.

articles.title: Poland invokes emergency grid capacity powers for second time in three days amid heatwave
articles.summaryB1: Poland has used emergency powers to manage its electricity grid for the second time in just three days. This happened during a period of very hot weather, called a heatwave. When temperatures rise sharply, people use much more electricity for cooling their homes and workplaces. This puts enormous pressure on the national grid, which is the system that moves electricity around the country. To prevent blackouts, the government can invoke special emergency measures. These measures allow authorities to limit how much electricity certain large users, such as factories, can consume. What makes this situation unusual is how often these powers have been used. Before this summer, Poland had only invoked them twice in the previous eight years. Using them twice in three days shows how serious the current situation is. Poland still relies heavily on coal-fired power stations, which have limits on how much electricity they can generate at peak times. The country is slowly moving toward renewable energy, but this transition takes time. For ordinary people, the heatwave is a reminder that climate change can affect daily life in practical ways. Energy experts say that investing in better grid infrastructure and more renewable sources could help Poland handle extreme weather events more effectively in the future.

articles.summaryB2: Poland has activated emergency grid capacity powers for the second time within three days, a response to the intense heatwave sweeping the country this summer. The frequency of these interventions is striking: prior to this summer, authorities had resorted to such measures only twice across an entire eight-year period. The rapid succession of activations signals that Poland's electricity infrastructure is struggling to cope with surging demand driven by extreme temperatures. During a heatwave, residential and industrial air conditioning systems run continuously, placing acute strain on the national transmission network. Emergency capacity measures typically allow grid operators to curtail electricity consumption among large industrial users, effectively rationing supply to prevent widespread outages. Poland's vulnerability in this situation is partly structural. The country remains heavily dependent on ageing coal-fired generation, which faces operational constraints precisely when demand peaks on the hottest days. Although Poland has accelerated investment in renewable energy in recent years, the pace of this transition has not kept up with the escalating frequency of extreme weather events attributed to climate change. Analysts warn that without substantial upgrades to both generation capacity and grid resilience, such emergency interventions may become routine rather than exceptional. The episode also reignites debate about the speed of Poland's energy transition and whether its current policy framework adequately addresses the climate-driven risks now manifesting in real time.

articles.title: Italians may help Germany get its trains to run on time
articles.summaryB1:
Germany is famous for many things, but punctual trains are not one of them. The country's rail network has had serious problems for years. Trains are often late, the infrastructure is old, and the national operator, Deutsche Bahn, has struggled to improve. Now, there may be a surprising solution: competition from Italian railway companies.

In recent years, European countries have been opening up their rail markets. This means that private companies from other countries can run trains on national networks. Italy did this earlier than most, and the results have been positive. An Italian company called Italo now competes with the state railway on busy routes. This competition has pushed both companies to offer better service and lower prices for passengers.

Germany is now trying a similar approach. Italian operators are interested in entering the German market and running services on some popular routes. Supporters believe that competition will force Deutsche Bahn to improve its reliability and become more efficient.

This matters because millions of Germans depend on trains every day. Better rail services would also help the environment, as more people might choose trains over cars or planes. The experience of other European countries shows that opening up national markets can bring real benefits. Germany's rail problems will not disappear overnight, but fresh competition could be a good starting point.

articles.questionB1: Do you think competition between railway companies can improve reliability and make public transport more efficient in Poland?
articles.summaryB2:
Germany's railway network has long been a source of national embarrassment. Deutsche Bahn, the state-owned operator, has accumulated a reputation for chronic delays, ageing infrastructure, and poor service quality. Despite repeated reform efforts, the system has remained stubbornly dysfunctional. Now, an unexpected model is attracting attention: the liberalisation of rail markets, with Italian operators potentially playing a starring role in Germany's recovery.

Italy liberalised its high-speed rail sector ahead of most European peers, allowing the privately-owned Italo to compete directly with the state-run Trenitalia on major intercity corridors. The outcome has been striking: fares dropped, punctuality improved, and passenger numbers rose. Proponents argue that this is a textbook illustration of how market liberalisation can galvanise a sluggish state monopoly into action.

Germany is now tentatively following this path. Under EU directives encouraging open access to national rail networks, Italian operators are reportedly eyeing lucrative German routes. The prospect of well-capitalised foreign competitors entering the market is seen by reformers as a potential catalyst for Deutsche Bahn to overhaul its operations.

Critics, however, warn that cherry-picking profitable intercity routes could leave rural and regional services underfunded, undermining the wider public transport mission. The debate reflects a tension at the heart of European rail policy: how to harness the dynamism of market forces while preserving universal access. Germany's experiment may yet offer instructive lessons for the entire continent.

articles.title: Sexually transmitted infections are surging in Europe
articles.summaryB1:
Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are increasing across Europe. Diseases like syphilis, gonorrhoea, and chlamydia are spreading more quickly than before, and health officials are worried. After years of progress in controlling these illnesses, the numbers are going in the wrong direction again.

There are several reasons for this rise. Many people do not get tested regularly, so they do not know they are infected. They can then pass the infection to others without realising it. Testing is not always easy to access, and some people feel ashamed to ask for help. This stigma stops many from visiting a doctor or a sexual health clinic.

Another problem is that some infections are becoming harder to treat. Certain bacteria are developing resistance to antibiotics, which means standard medicines no longer work as well.

To reduce the spread of STIs, health experts say countries must do two things. First, they must increase testing so that more people find out their status early. Second, they must reduce stigma so that people feel comfortable seeking help without embarrassment.

Public health campaigns can help change attitudes. When people feel safe and supported, they are more likely to get tested and treated. Governments across Europe need to invest more in sexual health services. The goal is to catch infections early and stop them from spreading further through communities.

articles.questionB1: Why do you think stigma makes it harder to control sexually transmitted infections, and how could communities reduce it?
articles.summaryB2:
Sexually transmitted infections are surging across Europe, reversing decades of hard-won public health progress. Cases of syphilis, gonorrhoea, and chlamydia have climbed sharply in recent years, alarming epidemiologists and policymakers alike. The resurgence reflects a complex mix of behavioural, systemic, and microbiological factors that no single intervention can easily address.

One major driver is chronic underdiagnosis. Because many STIs are asymptomatic in their early stages, a substantial portion of those infected remain unaware of their status, unwittingly transmitting the disease to partners. Patchy access to sexual health services — particularly in rural areas and among marginalised communities — compounds the problem. Underfunding of public health infrastructure over the past decade has left testing capacity strained in several countries.

Stigma remains a formidable barrier. Fear of judgement discourages individuals from seeking testing or disclosing their status to partners, allowing infections to circulate silently. Experts argue that destigmatising sexual health is not merely a social nicety but a clinical necessity, since shame-driven avoidance directly undermines containment efforts.

Complicating matters further is the emergence of antimicrobial resistance, particularly in gonorrhoea strains that no longer respond reliably to first-line antibiotics. This narrows the therapeutic options available to clinicians.

Health authorities across Europe are being urged to scale up testing programmes and launch targeted public awareness campaigns. The evidence is clear: early detection, paired with honest, non-judgmental outreach, offers the most effective path to curbing this resurgence before it becomes entrenched.

articles.title: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
articles.summaryB1:
Israel has rejected a peace plan from US President Donald Trump that included 15 points for ending the war in Gaza. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Israel's army will not leave Gaza until Hamas is 'genuinely' disarmed. This means Hamas must give up all its weapons before Israel agrees to pull out its troops.

The war in Gaza started after Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023. Since then, Israel has been carrying out military operations in Gaza. Many people have been killed and large parts of Gaza have been destroyed.

Trump's plan was an attempt to reach a ceasefire and bring peace to the region. However, Israel rejected the proposal because it does not believe Hamas will truly disarm. Netanyahu's government wants full control over the situation before withdrawing soldiers.

This decision makes it harder to end the conflict. Other countries and international organisations are worried about the humanitarian situation in Gaza, where many civilians do not have enough food, water, or medical care. The rejection of Trump's plan shows how difficult it is to reach an agreement when both sides have very different demands. The situation remains tense, and more talks are expected in the coming weeks.

articles.questionB1: Do you think a ceasefire is possible if both sides refuse to disarm or withdraw their forces? Why or why not?

Israel has formally rejected a 15-point peace framework put forward by US President Donald Trump aimed at bringing an end to the ongoing conflict in Gaza. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stated that Israeli forces would not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas had been 'genuinely' disarmed — a condition that effectively sets a very high bar for any negotiated settlement.

The rejection signals a hardening of Israel's stance and casts doubt on Washington's ability to broker a lasting agreement between the two sides. Trump's administration had presented the plan as a diplomatic pathway out of the conflict, which erupted following Hamas's deadly assault on Israel on 7 October 2023. Israel responded with an extensive military campaign that has devastated large parts of the Gaza Strip and resulted in a dire humanitarian crisis for the territory's civilian population.

Netanyahu's insistence on full disarmament before any Israeli pullout reflects deep-seated distrust of Hamas and domestic political pressure from hardline members of his coalition government. Critics argue that demanding complete disarmament as a precondition makes a negotiated outcome practically unachievable in the short term.

The impasse leaves Gaza's population in an increasingly desperate situation, with international aid agencies warning of severe shortages of food, medicine and clean water. Regional tensions remain high, and diplomats from multiple countries are expected to redouble efforts to find a compromise formula that could satisfy both parties.

articles.title: 'Spectacular' Game of Thrones stage spin-off opens at home of Shakespeare
articles.summaryB1: A new stage show based on the famous TV series Game of Thrones has opened at the Globe Theatre in London. The Globe is one of the most well-known theatres in the world. It was built close to the place where Shakespeare's original theatre stood hundreds of years ago. The show is called Game of Thrones: The Musical, and it is a spin-off, which means it is connected to the main story but tells a different part of it. Most theatre critics have given the show very positive reviews. They say it is a worthy addition to the Game of Thrones franchise, meaning it is good enough to be part of this popular series. Game of Thrones was one of the most watched TV shows in history. It was based on a series of fantasy novels and ran for eight seasons. Many fans were disappointed by the final season, so there has been a lot of pressure on new projects to succeed. This stage production seems to have impressed both critics and fans. It is described as spectacular, which means it looks and sounds amazing. The show gives fans a new way to experience the world of Game of Thrones. It also brings a big popular franchise to a historic theatre, which is an exciting combination for audiences.

articles.questionB1: Do you think a spectacular spin-off like this is a good way to keep a franchise alive after its original TV series has ended?
articles.summaryB2: A stage adaptation set within the Game of Thrones universe has made its debut at Shakespeare's Globe in London, drawing widespread acclaim from theatre critics who have largely hailed it as a worthy addition to the sprawling fantasy franchise. The production represents an intriguing convergence of high fantasy pop culture and one of Britain's most venerated theatrical institutions, a venue steeped in centuries of dramatic tradition. Most reviewers have responded with enthusiasm, describing the show as spectacular and praising its ambition in translating the visual grandeur of the television series into a live performance format. Game of Thrones, which aired from 2011 to 2019 and attracted a global audience of tens of millions, remains one of the most culturally pervasive television phenomena in recent memory. Its final season provoked considerable backlash among devoted fans, leaving the franchise with a somewhat tarnished legacy that subsequent projects have had to contend with. This stage spin-off appears to have navigated that challenge effectively, offering audiences a fresh perspective on the fictional world while benefiting from the prestige of its iconic venue. The choice of Shakespeare's Globe is itself a statement of intent — positioning the production not merely as fan service, but as a legitimate piece of theatrical storytelling. Whether it will sustain its momentum beyond the initial wave of critical goodwill remains to be seen.
