articles.questionB2: To what extent do you think the timing of the strikes represented a deliberate provocation, and how might such actions influence the decisions made at NATO summits?

articles.title: Three things you can do to stop EU border checks at the airport costing you
articles.summaryB1:
This summer, many travellers flying into or out of Europe may face long queues at airports. The reason is a new digital border control system introduced by the European Union. This system is called the Entry/Exit System, or EES. It collects fingerprints and photographs of non-EU citizens every time they cross an EU border. The aim is to improve security and track who enters and leaves the EU.

Before EES, border checks were quick for many passengers. Now, the process takes longer because border officers must register each traveller's data. This delay can cause queues to build up, especially at busy airports during peak travel times.

Experts and travel organisations have shared advice on how passengers can reduce the impact of these delays. First, you should arrive at the airport earlier than usual to allow extra time. Second, check whether your airport has dedicated EES lanes, as some airports have prepared better than others. Third, complete any pre-registration online if your country offers this option, as it can speed up the process at the border.

The new system affects British travellers in particular, because the UK is no longer part of the EU after Brexit. Understanding these changes and planning ahead can help you avoid stress and make sure your journey runs smoothly.

vocabularyB1.definition: The process of checking people as they enter or leave a country.
To officially record someone's information in a system.
The busiest periods when many people travel, like summer holidays.
Set apart for one specific purpose or group of people.
Thinking about and preparing for something before it happens.

articles.questionB1: How does planning ahead before a trip help you deal with new border control rules at airports?
articles.summaryB2:
European airports are bracing for significant disruption this summer following the imminent rollout of the EU's Entry/Exit System (EES), a biometric digital border control scheme designed to replace paper-stamped passports for non-EU nationals. The system records fingerprints, facial images and travel data each time a traveller crosses an external EU border, with the stated goal of tightening security and better monitoring overstays.

While the long-term rationale for EES is widely acknowledged, travel industry observers have flagged the real-world bottleneck it is likely to create at already-stretched airport checkpoints. Processing times per passenger are expected to increase considerably, raising the prospect of substantial queues during the summer peak season.

The BBC has outlined three practical steps travellers can take to mitigate the cost — both financial and practical — of these delays. Arriving at the airport well ahead of standard check-in windows is the first recommendation. Secondly, passengers are advised to check whether their departure or arrival airport has set up streamlined EES lanes, since infrastructure readiness varies considerably across member states. Finally, where available, completing pre-registration through an online portal in advance can expedite the in-person verification process.

The changes carry particular implications for British citizens, who became third-country nationals following Brexit and are therefore subject to full EES processing. For frequent flyers, factoring these procedural changes into travel planning is now a practical necessity rather than an optional precaution.

vocabularyB2.definition: Relating to unique physical characteristics, like fingerprints or facial features, used for identification.

To reduce the severity or negative effects of something.
To make a process happen faster or more efficiently.
People who are not citizens of any EU member state, treated as outsiders at EU borders.

articles.questionB2: Given that infrastructure readiness varies so widely across EU member states, how effectively can individual travellers mitigate the disruption caused by EES, and who bears the greater responsibility — governments or passengers?

articles.title: Parents warned not to publicly share children’s images amid AI abuse risks
articles.summaryB1:
The National Crime Agency (NCA) in the UK has warned parents to be careful about sharing photos of their children online. The NCA says that criminals are using artificial intelligence (AI) to turn innocent photos into child abuse material. This is a growing threat that many parents do not know about.

When parents post pictures of their children on social media, those images can be taken by bad people and changed using AI tools. The technology can create fake but realistic images that cause serious harm. This type of abuse is becoming more common as AI tools become easier to use.

The NCA is advising parents to think twice before they share any images of their children publicly. Private accounts and limited sharing are safer options. Parents should also check their privacy settings regularly.

This is not just a problem in the UK. It is a worldwide issue that governments and technology companies are trying to deal with. Child protection groups say that the law needs to catch up with the technology.

The warning reminds us that the internet can be a dangerous place for children, even when parents think they are simply sharing happy memories. Protecting children online requires awareness and careful choices about what we post and who can see it.

vocabularyB1.definition: Computer technology that can do tasks that normally need human thinking, like recognising images.
Content that shows harm done to someone, especially a child, in an illegal and harmful way.
Something dangerous that could cause harm or problems in the future.
Options on a website or app that control who can see your personal information or photos.
Knowledge and understanding of a situation or problem.

articles.questionB1: Now that you know about this threat, how do you think parents should change the way they share photos of their children online?
articles.summaryB2:
The UK's National Crime Agency (NCA) has issued a stark warning to parents, urging them to reconsider the practice of publicly sharing photographs of their children on social media. At the heart of the alert is a disturbing trend: criminals are exploiting artificial intelligence tools to manipulate innocent images into child sexual abuse material (CSAM), a phenomenon that experts say is escalating rapidly.

The technology in question allows offenders to take ordinary, publicly accessible photos and generate highly realistic fake abuse imagery. Because AI tools have become more widely available and easier to operate, the barrier to this type of offending has dropped considerably, widening the pool of potential perpetrators.

The NCA's guidance reflects a growing tension between parents' natural desire to document and celebrate their children's lives online and the very real dangers that public visibility can create. Authorities are recommending that parents restrict their profiles to trusted contacts and review their sharing habits carefully.

Child protection advocates argue that legislation has not kept pace with technological developments, leaving a regulatory gap that abusers are actively exploiting. Technology companies are also under pressure to detect and remove AI-generated abuse content more effectively.

The case highlights a broader challenge for modern societies: how to hold individuals, platforms, and lawmakers accountable in an era when digital tools can be weaponised against the most vulnerable. Protecting children in the digital age demands both personal vigilance and systemic action.

vocabularyB2.definition: Using something or someone unfairly or harmfully for personal gain or advantage.
People who commit a crime or harmful act.
A situation where laws or rules do not yet cover a new problem or technology.
Turned into a tool that is used to cause harm or damage, often in a new or unexpected way.
The practice of being very careful and watchful in order to notice and avoid danger.

articles.questionB2: Given the regulatory gap between existing legislation and rapidly evolving AI capabilities, who bears the greatest responsibility for protecting children from this form of digital exploitation — parents, platforms, or governments?

articles.title: The good tourist: can we learn to travel without absolutely infuriating the locals?
articles.summaryB1: Tourism is one of the biggest industries in the world, but it is causing serious problems. In 2023, around 1.3 billion people travelled across international borders as tourists. That is an enormous number, and many cities and communities are feeling the pressure. Local people in popular destinations are becoming angry. In Barcelona, protesters carried signs telling tourists to go home. Venice now charges visitors a fee to enter, and Amsterdam has closed its cruise ship terminal to reduce the number of visitors arriving by sea. The word "tourist" itself has a bad reputation. When someone calls you a tourist, it is rarely a compliment. It suggests that your interest in a place is shallow and that you do not really understand or respect it. Author Paige McClanahan believes there is a better way to travel. She argues that tourists should visit fewer places and spend more time in each destination. This approach could help reduce the damage that mass tourism causes to local communities and their culture. Instead of rushing through many cities, travellers could slow down, connect with local people, and spend their money in ways that actually benefit the community. McClanahan's ideas are part of a growing conversation about how we can enjoy travelling while also being respectful guests in the places we visit.

vocabularyB1.definition: A place that someone travels to on a holiday or trip
The opinion that people generally have about someone or something
Not showing serious thought or deep understanding of something
A polite remark that expresses praise or admiration for someone
To be helpful or useful to someone or something

articles.questionB1: Think about a popular tourist destination you know. How could tourists show more respect and actually benefit the local community?
articles.summaryB2: The global tourism industry is facing a backlash. In 2023, approximately 1.3 billion people crossed international borders as tourists — a figure representing an almost 25-fold increase compared to earlier decades and a full recovery from the Covid-era collapse. For many host communities, this sheer volume has become intolerable. Anti-tourism sentiment has hardened into organised resistance: Barcelona witnessed protest marches with placards bluntly demanding that tourists leave, Venice introduced an entry fee for day visitors, and Amsterdam's mayor moved to shut down the city's cruise ship terminal altogether. At the heart of the problem lies not just numbers, but attitude. The word "tourist" has long carried pejorative connotations — implying superficiality, ignorance, and a transactional relationship with place. That reputation has only worsened as overtourism has come to threaten housing affordability, cultural authenticity, and the daily lives of residents in sought-after cities. Author Paige McClanahan offers a potential remedy: what she calls being your "best self" abroad. Her prescription involves visiting fewer destinations and spending longer in each, allowing for deeper engagement with local people and economies. Rather than rushing between landmarks, McClanahan advocates a more deliberate form of travel — one that redistributes spending more equitably and leaves communities better off. Whether individual behaviour change can meaningfully address structural issues of overtourism, however, remains an open and contentious question.

vocabularyB2.definition: A word or expression that has a negative or disrespectful meaning or tone
A strong negative reaction from a group of people against something

articles.questionB2: McClanahan's approach places responsibility on individual travellers, yet overtourism is driven by structural economic forces. To what extent can a more equitable and deliberate style of travel realistically address this contentious global problem?

articles.title: Rolling Stones, deadites and pioneers: What to see, do or hear this week in Europe
articles.summaryB1:
This week in Europe, there are some exciting things happening in music and cinema. One of the biggest events is the release of a new album by The Rolling Stones. This famous British rock band has been making music since the 1960s. Their new album is their 25th studio record, which is a remarkable achievement for any musical group. The Rolling Stones are known all over the world for classic songs and energetic live performances. Fans have been waiting a long time for new material from the band.

In cinemas, a new horror film called 'Evil Dead Burn' is coming to the big screen. This movie is part of the well-known Evil Dead series, which has been popular with fans of scary films for decades. The story involves demonic creatures and plenty of dramatic action. Horror fans will recognise the style straight away.

These two releases show that European cultural life remains lively and full of variety. Whether you enjoy rock music or scary movies, there is something to look forward to this week. Events like these bring people together and give audiences a chance to experience new creative work. Keeping up with cultural releases is a great way to practise English and learn about the entertainment world at the same time.

articles.questionB1: Do you think a band's 25th studio record is an impressive achievement — and what makes a musical group stay popular for so long?
articles.summaryB2:
This week's European cultural calendar offers a striking contrast between rock legacy and horror revival. Most notably, The Rolling Stones are set to release their 25th album, a milestone that cements the band's extraordinary longevity in an industry notorious for burning through talent at speed. Having first emerged in the early 1960s, the Stones have outlasted countless contemporaries, reinventing themselves across generations without losing their devoted global fanbase. A new studio album at this stage of their career inevitably invites scrutiny — whether the record represents genuine artistic evolution or a well-crafted exercise in brand maintenance remains to be seen.

Meanwhile, on the big screen, 'Evil Dead Burn' arrives to satisfy audiences hungry for supernatural horror. The Evil Dead franchise has long occupied a distinctive niche in genre cinema, blending visceral scares with cult appeal. This latest instalment brings fresh demonic drama to a mythology that has endured since Sam Raimi's original 1981 film, demonstrating the franchise's remarkable resilience in an era of reboots and sequels.

Together, these two releases reflect a broader appetite for established cultural properties — audiences clearly find comfort and excitement in returning to familiar worlds, whether musical or cinematic. Yet both also carry the burden of expectation: the challenge of honouring a celebrated legacy while still surprising the people who know it best.

vocabularyB2.definition: The ability to last or remain active and successful for a very long time.

Producing a powerful, immediate emotional reaction that feels raw and instinctive.

Something valuable — such as a reputation or body of work — left behind by someone famous.

articles.questionB2: Given the resilience of both the Rolling Stones and the Evil Dead franchise, do you think cultural longevity is driven more by genuine artistic reinvention or by audiences' attachment to legacy?

articles.title: Donald Trump’s AI regime is opaque, unpredictable—and unsustainable
articles.summaryB1:
The United States government under President Donald Trump has taken control of who can use the most powerful artificial intelligence (AI) models. This means that companies and countries around the world must now get permission from the American administration before they can access the best AI systems.

This policy is very different from how AI was shared before. In the past, many AI tools were more openly available. Now, the government decides who gets access and who does not. This makes the system opaque, which means it is difficult to understand or see clearly how decisions are made.

The rules also change without much warning, so businesses and governments find the situation very unpredictable. They do not know what to expect next. This creates problems for companies that need to plan for the future.

Many experts believe this approach cannot last for a long time. They say it is unsustainable because other countries will develop their own powerful AI models, and American control will become weaker over time.

This matters for everyone, not just businesses. AI technology is changing how we work, communicate, and make decisions. When one government controls access to the best AI tools, it has enormous power over the global economy. People around the world are watching to see how this situation develops and whether fairer rules will be created.

vocabularyB1.definition: Difficult to understand or see clearly; not transparent or open
The ability or permission to use something or enter somewhere
The group of people who govern or manage a country or organisation
Official agreement that allows someone to do something
Something that cannot continue for a long time because it causes problems

articles.questionB1: Do you think one government should control access to powerful AI tools? What problems could this cause?
articles.summaryB2:
The Trump administration has moved to assert direct control over global access to the most advanced artificial intelligence models, marking a dramatic shift in how the United States manages its technological dominance. Under this regime, foreign companies and governments must seek American approval before using the most capable AI systems, effectively turning cutting-edge technology into a geopolitical instrument.

Critics and industry observers have highlighted two particular problems with this approach. First, the system is notably opaque: the criteria by which access is granted or denied remain poorly defined, leaving businesses unable to assess their standing or plan with confidence. Second, decisions appear highly unpredictable, shifting without clear rationale or advance notice. This volatility is particularly damaging for multinational corporations that depend on stable regulatory environments to make long-term investment decisions.

The Economist characterises the arrangement as unsustainable, and there are good reasons for this assessment. American hegemony over frontier AI models is unlikely to endure indefinitely. Rival powers, particularly China, are accelerating their own AI development programmes. As alternative models become more capable, the leverage Washington currently holds will erode, potentially undermining the entire framework of control.

There is also a broader commercial risk: companies frustrated by opaque rules may actively seek out non-American alternatives, inadvertently accelerating the fragmentation of the global AI ecosystem. Whether the administration can establish a more coherent and transparent framework before that happens remains an open and pressing question.

vocabularyB2.definition: Dominance or leadership of one country or group over others
A tendency to change suddenly and unpredictably, causing uncertainty
Relating to how geography and politics affect relationships between countries
To gradually weaken or wear something away over time
The process of breaking something into separate, disconnected pieces

articles.questionB2: Given the volatility of US AI policy, how might geopolitical rivals use this instability to accelerate their own AI programmes and challenge American technological dominance?

articles.title: Poland records highest ever temperature as European heatwave moves east
articles.summaryB1:
On Sunday, 28 June 2026, Poland recorded its highest ever temperature. A reading of 40.5°C (104.9°F) was measured in Słubice, a town in western Poland on the border with Germany. This broke all previous records in the country's history.

The extreme heat is part of a large heatwave that has been moving across Europe from west to east. Many other European countries experienced dangerously high temperatures before Poland. Such heatwaves can be deadly, especially for elderly people, young children, and those with health problems.

Slubice is a relatively small town, but its location in a flat, low-lying area may have contributed to the record temperature. Weather experts warned people to stay indoors during the hottest part of the day, drink plenty of water, and avoid direct sunlight.

High temperatures like this put pressure on hospitals and emergency services. They also cause damage to crops and increase the risk of wildfires in forests and dry areas.

Scientists say that heatwaves are becoming more frequent and more intense because of climate change. Every year, new temperature records are broken somewhere in the world. Events like this remind us why reducing carbon emissions and protecting the environment remain urgent global challenges. Poland's record temperature is a clear sign that no country in Europe is protected from extreme weather.

vocabularyB1.definition: A long period of unusually hot weather that can be dangerous to people.
The highest or lowest level ever measured or achieved.
Much greater or more severe than usual; far beyond normal.
The official line that separates two countries or regions.
Gases or substances released into the air, especially from burning fuel.

articles.questionB1: Why do you think extreme heatwaves are becoming more common, and what can ordinary people do to reduce carbon emissions in daily life?
articles.summaryB2:
Poland shattered its all-time temperature record on Sunday, 28 June 2026, when thermometers in the western border town of Słubice reached 40.5°C (104.9°F). The reading surpassed all previously documented highs in Polish meteorological history, marking a sobering milestone for a country not traditionally associated with Mediterranean-style heat.

The record came as an intense heatwave swept eastward across the continent, having already scorched large parts of Western and Central Europe in the days prior. Słubice, situated on the Oder River directly opposite the German town of Frankfurt an der Oder, sits in a low-lying region particularly susceptible to heat accumulation.

The public health ramifications of such temperatures are considerable. Authorities urged vulnerable groups — including the elderly, infants, and people with cardiovascular conditions — to limit outdoor exposure and maintain adequate hydration. Emergency services across affected regions reported surges in heat-related hospitalisations.

Beyond immediate human welfare, prolonged heat events of this magnitude pose a serious threat to agriculture, water supplies, and forest ecosystems, with the risk of wildfires escalating sharply as vegetation dries out.

Climate scientists attribute the rising frequency and severity of such episodes to anthropogenic climate change, noting that record-breaking temperatures are being documented with alarming regularity across Europe. Poland's new benchmark serves as a stark illustration of how rapidly the continent's climate is shifting, prompting fresh calls for accelerated action on emissions reduction and heat adaptation strategies.

vocabularyB2.definition: Went beyond a previous level or record; did better or more than before.
Related to the science of weather and the atmosphere.
The consequences or effects of an action or event, often complex or far-reaching.

articles.questionB2: Given that anthropogenic climate change is driving more frequent extremes, what ramifications might Poland's new temperature benchmark have for national policy on energy, public health, and urban planning?

articles.title: China cracks down on rule-bending offshore investments
articles.summaryB1:
China has introduced new rules to stop its citizens from putting money into foreign investments in ways that are not fully allowed by law. The government is especially worried about Chinese investors using special funds to buy shares in American technology companies. These funds, called QDII funds, are supposed to help Chinese people invest abroad legally. However, some investors have been bending the rules by paying extra money to get access to these funds beyond their official limits.

The Chinese government wants mainland investors to support Chinese technology companies instead. China has big dreams for its own tech industry and needs domestic investment to help these companies grow. Officials believe that money leaving the country to buy American tech stocks makes it harder to build a strong Chinese tech sector.

This crackdown is part of a wider effort by Beijing to control where Chinese money goes. The government regularly monitors capital flows, which means it watches how money moves in and out of the country. When too much money flows out, it can weaken the Chinese currency and reduce funds available for local businesses.

For ordinary Chinese investors, these new restrictions mean fewer chances to diversify their savings by buying foreign assets. Many people had hoped to benefit from the success of American tech giants. Now, the government is making it clear that it wants that investment to stay at home.

vocabularyB1.definition: Strong official action taken to stop something illegal or against the rules
To put money into something, hoping to make a profit later
Pools of money collected from many people and managed together
Related to your own country, not to foreign countries

articles.questionB1: Why might a government want domestic investors to keep their money inside the country instead of choosing to invest abroad?
articles.summaryB2:
China is tightening its grip on offshore investment flows, targeting a practice in which mainland investors circumvent official quotas to gain exposure to foreign — particularly American — technology stocks. The mechanism at the centre of the crackdown is the Qualified Domestic Institutional Investor (QDII) scheme, a government-approved channel that allows Chinese citizens to invest in overseas markets within strictly defined limits. Some investors, however, have been paying premiums on the secondary market to acquire QDII fund units beyond their allocated quotas, effectively bypassing the regulatory framework.

Beijing's move reflects a dual motivation. On one level, it is a routine exercise in capital controls, as authorities seek to limit outflows that could put downward pressure on the renminbi and drain liquidity from domestic markets. On another level, it signals a deliberate industrial policy ambition: Chinese regulators appear determined to channel private savings toward homegrown technology champions rather than rivals in Silicon Valley.

This tension between investor preference and state direction illustrates a recurring theme in China's financial system. Ordinary savers, frustrated by sluggish returns in domestic markets, have sought offshore exposure as a means of portfolio optimisation. The government, by contrast, views speculative outflows as a distraction from its strategic goal of building self-sufficient technology industries.

The implications for Chinese retail investors are tangible. Access to global markets will narrow further, limiting the ability to hedge against domestic economic uncertainty. Meanwhile, companies in China's tech sector stand to benefit from a more captive pool of investment capital.

vocabularyB2.definition: To find a clever way to avoid a rule or restriction without directly breaking it

Government restrictions on how money can move in or out of a country

Describing a market or group that has no real freedom to choose alternatives

articles.questionB2: To what extent do China's capital controls reflect genuine financial stability concerns, and to what extent are they a tool to direct speculative investment toward state-preferred industries?

articles.title: Is too much sleep as bad as too little?
articles.summaryB1:
Most people know that sleeping too little is bad for their health. But new research suggests that sleeping too much might also be harmful. Scientists are now trying to find out how much sleep is actually best for us.

Studies show that adults who sleep for seven to eight hours a night tend to be the healthiest. People who regularly sleep for nine hours or more have a higher risk of serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes. This pattern appears in many different countries and age groups.

However, scientists are not sure whether too much sleep causes these problems, or whether people sleep more because they are already ill. This is a difficult question to answer. Some researchers think that long sleep is a symptom of other conditions, not the cause.

There is also the question of sleep quality. Deep, restful sleep is very different from light, broken sleep. Someone who spends ten hours in bed but wakes up many times may not actually be getting enough proper rest.

Understanding the optimal amount of sleep is not simple. Our bodies are all different, and individual needs vary. Age, lifestyle, and genetics all play a role. Experts recommend that most adults aim for seven to nine hours of good-quality sleep each night to maintain their wellbeing.

vocabularyB1.definition: Causing damage or injury to your body or health.
A sign that shows you may have an illness or health problem.
The best or most suitable amount or level of something.
Relaxing and helping you to feel rested and refreshed.
The general state of being healthy, comfortable, and happy.

articles.questionB1: What changes could you make to your daily routine to get more restful sleep and improve your overall wellbeing?
articles.summaryB2:
The conventional wisdom that sleep deprivation poses serious health risks is well established, but emerging research is complicating the picture by suggesting that excessive sleep may be equally detrimental. Scientists are now engaged in the tricky business of determining the optimal sleep window — and why straying beyond it in either direction appears to carry measurable consequences.

Epidemiological data consistently link sleeping nine hours or more per night with elevated rates of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and premature mortality. Yet researchers face a persistent methodological challenge: the direction of causality is far from clear. It remains plausible that prolonged sleep is not itself the culprit but rather a manifestation of underlying conditions — depression, chronic inflammation, or undiagnosed illness — that also happen to increase sleep duration.

A further complication is the distinction between sleep quantity and sleep quality. Spending extended hours in bed does not guarantee restorative sleep; fragmented or shallow sleep may leave the body equally compromised, regardless of total duration. Wearable technology and polysomnography are beginning to give researchers more granular data, but translating laboratory findings into reliable public health guidance remains an ongoing challenge.

The emerging consensus points to seven to nine hours as the sweet spot for most adults, though individual variation driven by genetics and age means that blanket recommendations can only go so far. Understanding why the upper boundary exists may ultimately prove as revealing as decades of research into the harms of sleep deprivation.

articles.title: Cold feet: could putting your socks in the fridge help you through the heatwave?
articles.summaryB1: When the weather is very hot, many people struggle to sleep and feel comfortable. One simple trick that experts are now recommending is putting your socks in the fridge before wearing them. According to the Red Cross, this method can actually help your body cool down during a heatwave. But why does it work? The answer is connected to how our bodies control temperature. Our feet have many blood vessels near the skin, so cooling them down can help reduce our overall body heat quite quickly. This is the same reason why putting your feet in cold water feels so refreshing on a hot day. The idea might sound strange at first, but health organisations say it is worth trying. Heatwaves are becoming more common in many parts of Europe, including countries that are not used to very high temperatures. People in these places often do not have air conditioning at home, so finding cheap and easy ways to stay cool is very useful. Keeping cold socks in the fridge costs nothing and needs no special equipment. Experts suggest wearing them for about twenty minutes before bed. It may not solve every problem caused by extreme heat, but it can make a real difference to how comfortable you feel.

vocabularyB1.definition: A period of unusually hot weather that lasts for several days
Tubes inside the body that carry blood around
Making you feel cool, comfortable, and less tired
A system that cools the air inside a building or car
Temperatures that are much hotter than normal and can be dangerous

articles.questionB1: Would you try wearing cold socks during a heatwave to stay cool, or do you prefer other ways to deal with extreme heat?
articles.summaryB2: As Europe endures increasingly severe summers, a somewhat unconventional piece of advice has emerged from an authoritative source: the Red Cross is advocating the practice of chilling your socks in the refrigerator before wearing them as a practical strategy for surviving a heatwave. The recommendation may initially strike readers as whimsical, yet there is genuine physiological reasoning behind it. The feet contain a dense network of blood vessels positioned close to the skin's surface, meaning that applying cold to this area can trigger a rapid reduction in core body temperature — a process known as peripheral cooling. This is the same mechanism that makes immersing your feet in cold water so immediately effective on a sweltering day. The article, published in a lighthearted question-and-answer format by The Guardian, takes a playful approach to what is, in reality, a pressing public health matter. Northern and central European countries, including those unaccustomed to prolonged periods of intense heat, face a particular challenge: the vast majority of households lack air conditioning, leaving residents to improvise with low-cost remedies. The chilled sock method requires no financial outlay and no specialist knowledge, making it genuinely accessible to vulnerable groups such as the elderly, who are disproportionately affected by heat-related illness. Whether such household tips can meaningfully offset the dangers of extreme temperatures remains an open question, but they represent a practical, immediate response while systemic solutions lag behind.

articles.title: Going to a festival as a neurodivergent person can be tough - but there are ways to recharge
articles.summaryB1:
Music festivals are exciting events, but they can be very difficult for people who are neurodivergent. Neurodivergent people have brains that work differently from most people. This includes people with autism, ADHD, or anxiety. At festivals, there is often loud music, large crowds, and bright lights. These things can feel overwhelming and cause great stress or discomfort for neurodivergent people.

Some festivals are now trying to help. They are offering calm spaces where people can go to rest and recover from the noise and crowds. Some events are also providing noise-cancelling headphones, which block out loud sounds and make the environment more comfortable. These are devices you wear over your ears to reduce unwanted noise.

However, many people think that festivals need to do much more. There are growing calls from disability advocates and neurodivergent communities for better support and more inclusive planning. They want festivals to think carefully about the needs of all visitors, not just those without disabilities.

This topic matters because millions of people around the world are neurodivergent. Everyone deserves the chance to enjoy live music and cultural events. Making festivals more accessible is a step towards a fairer society. Small changes, like quiet rooms and sensory-friendly options, can make a huge difference to people who might otherwise feel excluded from these popular events.

vocabularyB1.definition: A person whose brain works differently, for example someone with autism or ADHD
Too much to deal with; causing strong feelings of stress or confusion
Quiet areas at an event where people can rest and feel safe
Devices worn over the ears that block or reduce loud sounds around you
Easy for everyone to use or enjoy, including people with disabilities

articles.questionB1: What calm spaces or other changes would make festivals more accessible and enjoyable for neurodivergent people in your country?
articles.summaryB2:
Music festivals have long been celebrated as communal experiences of joy and self-expression, yet for neurodivergent individuals — those with conditions such as autism, ADHD, or sensory processing differences — they can represent an ordeal of competing stimuli. Relentless noise, dense crowds, unpredictable schedules, and flashing lights create an environment that many find deeply distressing rather than exhilarating.

In response to growing awareness, some festival organisers have begun rolling out practical accommodations: dedicated calm spaces where attendees can decompress away from sensory overload, and noise-cancelling headphones available for loan. These provisions are welcomed by neurodivergent communities as a step in the right direction.

Nevertheless, advocates argue that such measures remain piecemeal and fall well short of genuine inclusion. There are vocal calls to go further — to embed neurodivergent-friendly design into the core planning of events, rather than treating it as an afterthought. This could include clearer visual guides, quieter viewing zones, and more transparent communication about what attendees can expect.

The debate reflects a wider cultural shift in how public events consider disability and difference. Proponents of more ambitious reform contend that accessibility should not be a bolt-on feature but a foundational principle. Given that neurodivergent people represent a substantial portion of the population, the argument is compelling: festivals that fail to accommodate diverse neurological needs risk excluding a significant number of potential attendees from cultural life altogether.

articles.questionB2: To what extent should festival organisers be legally required to provide accommodations for neurodivergent attendees, and who should bear responsibility when such provisions remain piecemeal?

articles.title: Europe's heatwave linked to 1,300 deaths, WHO says, as Germany hits record 41.7C
articles.summaryB1: Europe has been hit by a very dangerous heatwave, and the World Health Organization (WHO) says it has been linked to at least 1,300 deaths. The WHO chief, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, warned that Europe is not ready to deal with such extreme heat. Germany recorded its highest ever temperature of 41.7 degrees Celsius during this period, which is a serious public health emergency. A heatwave happens when temperatures stay much higher than normal for several days. Older people, young children, and those with health problems are especially at risk during these events. High temperatures can cause heatstroke, which happens when the body gets too hot and cannot cool itself down. Doctors advise people to drink plenty of water, stay in the shade, and avoid going outside during the hottest part of the day. Governments across Europe are being urged to take action to protect their citizens. Climate experts say that heatwaves are becoming more frequent and more deadly because of climate change. This means that countries need to prepare better systems to warn people about dangerous temperatures and to provide cool shelter for those who need it. The WHO warning is a clear sign that Europe must treat extreme heat as a serious threat to public health.

vocabularyB1.definition: A period of unusually hot weather lasting several days or longer

Temperatures that are dangerously much higher than normal
A dangerous condition when the body becomes too hot and stops working properly
A place that protects people from danger or bad weather

articles.questionB1: What do you think governments should do to protect people from extreme heat during a heatwave?
articles.summaryB2: The World Health Organization has attributed at least 1,300 deaths across Europe to an intense heatwave, with WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus issuing a stark warning that the continent is fundamentally ill-equipped to cope with soaring temperatures. The alarm was sounded as Germany shattered its all-time temperature record, reaching 41.7 degrees Celsius — a figure that alarmed meteorologists and public health officials alike. The WHO's assessment reflects a growing body of evidence that heatwaves represent one of the most lethal consequences of climate change, disproportionately affecting vulnerable populations such as the elderly, those with pre-existing medical conditions, and people without access to adequate cooling. Ghebreyesus's warning carries particular weight given Europe's historically temperate climate, which means that infrastructure, housing, and healthcare systems were simply not designed with prolonged extreme heat in mind. Unlike regions accustomed to high temperatures, much of northern and central Europe lacks air conditioning in homes, hospitals, and public buildings, leaving residents acutely exposed. Public health specialists argue that heat emergency plans, including early warning systems and the designation of cooling centres, must become standard policy across member states. The record-breaking temperatures in Germany serve as a sobering reminder that climate adaptation is no longer a distant priority but an immediate necessity, demanding coordinated action from governments, urban planners, and healthcare providers across the continent.

articles.questionB2: Given that Europe's temperate climate has historically shaped its infrastructure and healthcare systems, how should policymakers prioritise climate adaptation to protect populations disproportionately at risk from heatwaves?

articles.title: Trump threatens 100% tariff on European nations over tech tax
articles.summaryB1: US President Donald Trump has threatened to put a 100% tariff on goods from European countries. A tariff is an extra tax that a country charges on products coming in from other countries. Trump made this threat because several European nations are thinking about creating a new tax on technology companies. Many of these companies are American, such as Google and Amazon. Trump says this kind of tax is unfair to the United States. If European countries bring in the tech tax, American products sold in Europe would become twice as expensive because of the 100% tariff. This would make it much harder for US companies to sell their goods in Europe. A trade dispute like this could affect businesses and consumers on both sides. Prices for many products could go up. European governments have not yet responded officially to Trump's warning. However, this is not the first time Trump has used tariffs as a way to put pressure on other countries. He has done the same with China and Canada. The situation shows how technology and trade are becoming connected in global politics. Both sides will need to find a way to talk and reach an agreement before the conflict gets worse.

articles.questionB1: Do you think using tariffs as pressure is a fair way for countries to solve disagreements, or should they find other solutions?
articles.summaryB2: President Donald Trump has escalated tensions with Europe by threatening to impose a 100% tariff on goods imported from European nations. The move came in response to discussions among several European governments about introducing a digital services tax targeting large technology corporations — most of which are American. Trump framed the proposed levy as discriminatory, arguing it unfairly singles out US firms operating in European markets. A 100% tariff would effectively double the cost of European exports to the United States, a retaliatory measure that could have serious economic consequences for both sides. Critics warn that such an aggressive stance risks triggering a full-scale trade war at a time when the global economy is already under strain. Supporters, however, argue that Trump is defending American commercial interests against what they see as protectionist policies from European governments. The digital services tax debate is not new — European countries have long argued that tech giants generate enormous profits on their soil while paying relatively little in local taxes. The OECD has been working on a multilateral framework to address this imbalance, but progress has been slow. Trump's threat adds fresh urgency to those talks, while simultaneously making diplomatic resolution more difficult. Whether the two sides can reach a compromise without further escalating the confrontation remains to be seen.

articles.questionB2: Given the slow progress of multilateral efforts to reform digital taxation, do you think Trump's retaliatory tariff threat is more likely to accelerate a solution or deepen the divide between the US and Europe?

articles.title: Global warming has made Europe’s heatwave 2-4°C worse
articles.summaryB1:
Europe is experiencing a severe heatwave in the summer of 2026. Scientists say that climate change has made this heatwave between 2 and 4 degrees Celsius hotter than it would have been without global warming. This finding comes from a field of science called attribution science, which tries to measure how much human-caused climate change affects extreme weather events.

Europe is warming faster than any other continent on Earth. This means that heatwaves in Europe are becoming more frequent and more intense over time. High temperatures can be very dangerous, especially for older people and those with health problems. They can also damage crops and cause wildfires.

Scientists use climate models to compare what actually happened with what might have happened in a world without greenhouse gas emissions. By doing this, they can calculate how much worse a heatwave is because of human activity.

This matters because it shows a clear link between the burning of fossil fuels and extreme heat. Governments and individuals need to understand this connection. Reducing emissions could help limit future heatwaves. If the world does not act, temperatures will continue to rise, and extreme heat events will become even more dangerous. Europe must prepare for a hotter future by building better infrastructure and protecting vulnerable populations.

vocabularyB1.definition: A long period of unusually hot weather that can be dangerous to people.
Gases, especially carbon dioxide, released into the air by cars, factories, and burning fuel.

Basic systems a country needs to work, such as roads, buildings, and water supply.

articles.questionB1: How might more frequent and intense heatwaves affect vulnerable people in your country, and what should governments do about rising emissions?
articles.summaryB2:
A powerful heatwave swept across Europe in June 2026, and scientists have now concluded that human-driven climate change made it between 2 and 4 degrees Celsius hotter than it would otherwise have been. The finding comes from rapid attribution studies, a methodology that has matured considerably over the past decade, allowing researchers to quantify the fingerprint of global warming on specific extreme weather events within days of their occurrence.

The conclusions are particularly alarming given that Europe is warming faster than any other continent, a trend that scientists attribute to a combination of geographical factors and shifts in atmospheric circulation patterns. This accelerated warming means that European populations are disproportionately exposed to heat stress compared with other parts of the world at similar latitudes.

Attribution science works by running climate models thousands of times, both with and without observed greenhouse gas concentrations, then comparing outcomes statistically. The difference between these two scenarios reveals how much more extreme an event was made by anthropogenic emissions. Critics of the approach note that such models carry inherent uncertainties, but the scientific consensus strongly supports the general direction of the findings.

The implications extend well beyond public health. Agriculture, energy systems, and urban planning all face mounting pressure as extreme heat becomes more frequent. Policymakers are now under growing pressure to accelerate decarbonisation efforts and invest in adaptation strategies, recognising that mitigation alone may no longer be sufficient to protect European societies from the consequences of a rapidly warming planet.

Caused or produced by human activity, especially pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.
To a degree that is larger or smaller than would normally be expected or considered fair.

Actions taken to reduce the severity or harmful effects of something, such as climate change.

articles.questionB2: Given the inherent uncertainties in climate attribution studies, how should policymakers balance the urgent need for decarbonisation with the economic costs of rapid systemic change in Europe?

articles.title: California’s landmark anti-plastics law sparks anger as 17 states move to sue
articles.summaryB1: A new law in California is making big changes to how plastic packaging is made. The law was signed by Governor Gavin Newsom in 2022 but only came into effect in May 2025. It requires companies that make plastic packaging to use less single-use plastic. Single-use plastic is plastic that is used only once and then thrown away, like bottles or food wrappers. By 2032, all packaging must be either recyclable or compostable, meaning it can be broken down naturally in the ground. The main goal is to incentivize producers to think about what happens to their products after people use them. This should lead to better, more sustainable packaging in the future. However, the law is already causing anger. The chemicals industry does not like it because it will cost them money and change how they work. At the same time, environmental groups say the law does not go far enough and is too timid. To make things more complicated, 17 American states are planning to sue, which means they want to take legal action to stop the law. This story shows how difficult it can be to phase out old habits and materials, even when the goal is to protect the environment.

articles.questionB1: Should governments incentivize companies to phase out single-use plastics, or should individual people change their habits first?
articles.summaryB2: California's ambitious legislation requiring plastic packaging producers to eliminate single-use plastics has ignited controversy from multiple sides just weeks after coming into force. Signed by Governor Gavin Newsom in 2022 but only enacted in May 2025, the law mandates that plastic and packaging companies reduce their reliance on single-use materials and ensure that all packaging is either recyclable or compostable by 2032. The underlying rationale is to compel producers to factor in the full lifecycle of their products, thereby driving innovation toward genuinely sustainable alternatives in bottles, containers and wrappings. Yet the law finds itself under fire from opposing camps. The chemicals industry has reacted with hostility, viewing the regulations as commercially damaging and overreaching, and seventeen US states are preparing to sue in an attempt to overturn or block the legislation. From the opposite direction, environmental groups have criticised the law as too timid, arguing that it does not go nearly far enough in tackling the scale of plastic pollution. This tension between industry opposition and environmentalist dissatisfaction reflects a familiar pattern in green policymaking: ambitious legislation often struggles to satisfy either side. California has long acted as a regulatory trailblazer in the United States, and the outcome of these legal challenges could have far-reaching consequences for how other states approach the contentious issue of plastic waste reduction.

articles.questionB2: Given that the law is simultaneously criticised as too weak by environmentalists and too restrictive by industry, what does this tension reveal about the contentious nature of legislating for environmental change?

articles.title: Europe’s foreign policy turf war
articles.summaryB1: The European Union has many people who work on foreign policy. But who is really in charge? This is a question that causes arguments inside the EU. Different institutions and officials all want to have power over how Europe deals with other countries. The European Commission, the Council of the EU, and individual member states often disagree about who should speak for Europe on the world stage. This is sometimes called a 'turf war' – a fight over who controls a particular area of work. For example, when Europe needs to respond to a crisis, different officials may give different messages. This can make the EU look weak or confused to other countries. The problem is that the EU's system of foreign policy is very complicated. There are many overlapping roles and it is not always clear who has the final say. For Polish citizens, this matters because Poland is an active EU member state that cares deeply about European security and its relationship with neighbours like Ukraine and Russia. If the EU cannot speak with one voice in foreign policy, it may struggle to protect European interests. Understanding how power is shared – and fought over – inside the EU helps us understand why European foreign policy sometimes moves slowly or sends mixed messages to the world.

articles.questionB1: When different institutions send mixed messages about foreign policy, what problems can this cause for the EU on the world stage?
articles.summaryB2: A simmering dispute over who holds authority in European Union foreign policy has once again come to the fore, exposing deep-seated tensions between the EU's competing power centres. The European Commission, the Council of the EU, and individual member states have long jostled for influence over how Europe presents itself to the world – a contest that critics argue undermines the bloc's credibility as a unified geopolitical actor. At the heart of the matter is an inherently ambiguous institutional architecture, in which multiple officials hold overlapping mandates with no clear hierarchy. The EU's High Representative for Foreign Affairs, the European Commission President, and national foreign ministers frequently operate on parallel tracks, occasionally contradicting one another in public. This fragmentation is more than a procedural inconvenience. In an era defined by Russia's war in Ukraine, strained transatlantic relations, and growing assertiveness from China, the EU's inability to project a coherent voice carries real strategic costs. Member states with strong national foreign policy traditions – including France and Germany – are often reluctant to cede ground to supranational bodies, further complicating efforts at coordination. For countries like Poland, which sits on NATO's eastern flank and has a direct stake in European security arrangements, the question of who speaks for Europe is far from abstract. The turf war at the top of EU diplomacy is, ultimately, a reflection of the unresolved tension between integration and sovereignty that has defined the European project since its inception.

articles.title: Social media bans go global: big tech faces a reckoning after Australia’s crackdown
articles.summaryB1: Many countries around the world are now trying to limit how much time children spend on social media. This movement started gaining serious attention after Australia introduced a ban on social media for people under the age of 16. The Australian law was one of the strictest of its kind, and it sent a clear message to big technology companies that governments are willing to act. Now other countries are looking at similar rules to protect young people online. Supporters of these bans say that social media can harm children's mental health and that companies have not done enough to keep young users safe. Critics, however, worry that bans are too difficult to enforce and may not actually solve the problem. Some people compare this moment to the fight against the tobacco industry, when governments finally stepped in to regulate something many people had enjoyed for years. The phrase 'big tobacco moment' suggests that technology companies may soon face the same kind of strict rules that cigarette makers had to follow. Whether these bans will work is still unclear, but it seems that governments around the world are no longer willing to ignore the issue. The pressure on tech companies to change how they operate is growing fast.

articles.questionB1: Do you think governments should ban children from using social media to protect them, or are there better ways to keep young people safe online?
articles.summaryB2: A growing number of governments worldwide are moving to rein in children's access to social media platforms, following Australia's landmark decision to prohibit users under 16 from joining these services. The Australian legislation, widely regarded as among the most sweeping of its kind, has emboldened other nations to consider comparable measures, signalling a potential turning point in how states relate to the tech industry. What is clear is that the political will to act appears to be hardening across multiple continents, and technology companies are under mounting scrutiny from regulators who seem less inclined than ever to accept self-regulation as a sufficient response.

articles.title: Airbus under fresh scrutiny as EASA orders A380 inspections over wing cracks
articles.summaryB1: Airbus, one of the world's biggest makers of passenger planes, is facing new problems. EASA is the official body responsible for making sure that aircraft in Europe are safe to fly. Airlines that operate the A380 must now carry out these checks and report their findings. This is not the only difficulty Airbus is dealing with at the moment. The company is also struggling with supply chain problems, which means it is having trouble getting the parts and materials it needs to build new planes. The situation shows how even the most successful companies in the aviation industry can face serious challenges at the same time.

articles.questionB1: If you were an airline manager, how would you reassure passengers after regulators ordered safety inspections of your planes?
articles.summaryB2: The European Union Aviation Safety Agency has issued a directive ordering airlines worldwide to conduct mandatory inspections of Airbus A380 aircraft following the discovery of cracks in the wings of several planes. articles.title: Tech stocks tumble on concerns over AI spending
articles.summaryB1:
Tech stocks fell sharply this week after news about a new, cheaper Chinese AI model caused investors to worry about the future of AI spending. A Chinese company called DeepSeek released an AI assistant that reportedly costs much less to run than similar American products. This news made people question whether big US tech companies need to spend so much money building AI systems.

Shares in major technology firms dropped quickly. Nvidia, a company that makes computer chips used in AI, saw its share price fall by almost 17% in a single day. This was one of the biggest one-day losses in stock market history.

Investors have been pouring billions of dollars into AI technology, believing it will bring huge profits in the future. However, the arrival of a cheap rival product triggered doubt about this plan. If AI can be built more cheaply, companies may not need to buy as many expensive chips or build as many large data centres.

This story matters because many people's savings and pension funds are connected to tech stocks. When share prices fall sharply, it can affect ordinary people too. It also shows how quickly the tech industry can change. A single announcement from a rival company can shake confidence in the entire market and trigger a wave of selling across the world.

vocabularyB1.definition: Shares in technology companies that people buy and sell on the stock market.

articles.questionB1: If a rival company can build AI more cheaply, do you think investors were right to sell their tech stocks so quickly? Why or why not?
articles.summaryB2:
Global technology stocks suffered a dramatic sell-off this week, wiping hundreds of billions of dollars off market valuations, after the emergence of DeepSeek, a Chinese artificial intelligence model that appears to match the capabilities of leading US products at a fraction of the cost. The development sent shockwaves through financial markets, prompting investors to reassess the astronomical levels of capital expenditure that American tech giants have committed to AI infrastructure.

Nvidia bore the brunt of the turmoil, with its share price plummeting by roughly 17% in a single session — one of the steepest single-day declines ever recorded for a company of its scale. The chipmaker's products are central to training large AI models, so any suggestion that AI development could be achieved more efficiently threatens its core revenue model.

The episode has reignited a long-running debate about whether the current wave of AI investment is sustainable. Tech companies such as Microsoft, Meta, and Google have pledged staggering sums to build data centres and acquire hardware. If DeepSeek's low-cost approach proves replicable at scale, analysts warn that this spending rationale may be fundamentally flawed.

From a geopolitical perspective, DeepSeek's ascent also highlights the intensifying competition between the US and China in AI development, particularly given that American export restrictions were designed to limit China's access to advanced chips. The turmoil in markets reflects not just financial anxiety, but a deeper uncertainty about who will ultimately define the future of artificial intelligence.

India is already one of the biggest markets for WhatsApp, with hundreds of millions of people using it every day to send messages, share photos, and make calls. Meta believes that having a leader with strong connections to India will help the app grow even more there. WhatsApp is not just a messaging tool in India — many people use it for business and to stay in touch with family. The new leader comes from a start-up background, which means they have experience building something new and making it successful. This kind of experience could help WhatsApp reach even more users across India. The leadership change shows how much Meta values the Indian market. As smartphones become cheaper and more people go online in India, the opportunity for WhatsApp to expand its presence there is very real.

articles.title: You’re only supposed to blow the bloody hooves off: AI Michael Caine narrates Odyssey audiobook

The title of the Guardian article about this audiobook is a funny joke. articles.title: Seabed damaged by fishing showing signs of recovery
articles.summaryB1:
An area of the sea near the English coast is showing signs of recovery after it was badly damaged by illegal fishing. The seabed in this protected area was damaged by boats using a method called dredging, which involves dragging heavy equipment along the ocean floor to collect shellfish. This destroys the natural environment and harms the creatures that live there.

The area is officially a marine protected zone, which means fishing activities like dredging are not allowed there. However, illegal dredging still happened and caused serious damage to the seabed and the species that depend on it.

Now, campaigners and environmental groups are reporting that the seabed is beginning to recover. They say this is proof that marine protection works when rules are followed. Animals and plants are returning to the area, and the natural habitat is slowly rebuilding itself.

This news is encouraging for people who campaign for stronger ocean protection laws. They argue that governments need to do more to enforce the rules in protected areas and stop illegal fishing from happening.

The recovery of this seabed shows that nature can heal itself if humans give it the chance. Experts believe that protecting more ocean areas could help restore damaged ecosystems and support the long-term health of our seas.

People who work actively to change something in society, often about environment or rights
To make sure people follow rules or laws, using official power if necessary
The natural place where an animal or plant normally lives and grows

articles.questionB1: Do you think governments do enough to enforce rules in marine protected zones, and what more could they do?
articles.summaryB2:
A stretch of English seabed that was illegally ravaged by commercial dredging is now displaying encouraging signs of ecological recovery, according to environmental campaigners. The area in question lies within a designated marine protected zone, where bottom-trawling and dredging are explicitly prohibited due to the devastating impact these practices have on seabed habitats and the biodiversity they support.

Despite its protected status, the site fell victim to illegal dredging operations, which strip the ocean floor of its structure, destroy fragile ecosystems, and displace or kill the species that inhabit them. The violation drew sharp criticism from conservation groups, who argued that inadequate monitoring and weak enforcement had allowed such destruction to occur unchecked.

However, follow-up surveys now suggest that the seabed is beginning to regenerate, with native species returning and reef-like structures slowly re-establishing themselves. Campaigners are seizing on this evidence to argue that marine protection is not merely symbolic — when properly upheld, it demonstrably works.

The case has reignited debate about how governments monitor and police protected marine areas. Conservationists argue that without meaningful consequences for violations, designated zones offer little more than paper protection. They are calling for increased surveillance, tougher penalties, and greater political will to safeguard ocean ecosystems.

For advocates of ocean conservation, the partial recovery of this site offers a measured but genuine reason for optimism — and a concrete argument for expanding marine protections globally.

articles.questionB2: Given that this marine protected zone suffered illegal dredging despite its designated status, what does this reveal about the gap between paper protection and genuine conservation in practice?

articles.title: Cristiano Ronaldo scores at his sixth World Cup
articles.summaryB1: Cristiano Ronaldo has made history at the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The Portuguese football star scored a goal for Portugal in their group match against Uzbekistan, which was played in Houston, USA. Portugal won the game. This moment was special because Ronaldo became the first footballer ever to score at six different World Cup tournaments. A tournament is a competition where many teams play against each other to find the best one. Ronaldo first played at the World Cup in 2006, when he was just 21 years old. Since then, he has appeared at every tournament, showing incredible dedication to his sport. He is now in his 40s, which makes this achievement even more remarkable. Most professional footballers retire before reaching this age, so Ronaldo's ability to compete at the highest level is extraordinary. Portugal is one of the strongest teams in the competition this year, and Ronaldo's record-breaking goal gives the team confidence. Fans around the world celebrated this moment, recognising that they were watching something that had never happened before in football history. Whether Portugal can go on to win the tournament remains to be seen, but Ronaldo has already left his mark on these World Cup games.

articles.questionB1: What does Ronaldo's remarkable achievement at six World Cup tournaments tell us about dedication in professional sport?
articles.summaryB2: Cristiano Ronaldo etched his name further into football folklore at the 2026 FIFA World Cup, becoming the first player in the history of the sport to score at six separate World Cup tournaments. The milestone came during Portugal's group-stage victory over Uzbekistan in Houston, a match that served as the backdrop for yet another chapter in the Portuguese forward's extraordinary career. Ronaldo, who made his World Cup debut in Germany in 2006, has now spanned two decades of the sport's most prestigious competition, a feat that speaks to both his exceptional longevity and his relentless physical conditioning at an age when most elite athletes have long since retired. The record places Ronaldo in uncharted territory, beyond the reach of legends such as Pelé and Diego Maradona, who never had the opportunity to compete across such an extended timeline. Critics who had questioned whether Ronaldo deserved a place in the squad ahead of younger, emerging talent were at least temporarily silenced by the goal. From a broader sporting perspective, the achievement invites reflection on what it means to sustain elite performance over generations, and on how modern sports science and nutrition have redefined the boundaries of athletic ageing. articles.title: Meta halts worker tracking for AI training due to privacy fears
articles.summaryB1: Meta, the company that owns Facebook and Instagram, has stopped a programme that tracked how its workers used their computers. The programme began only two months ago. Meta wanted to collect data from employees' computer activity to help train its artificial intelligence systems. However, workers and privacy groups raised serious worries about this practice. They felt it was not right for a company to monitor its employees so closely without clear consent. Privacy means the right to keep personal information private and under your own control. Many people believe that collecting data from workers without full agreement is a violation of their rights. Meta decided to halt the programme after these concerns became public. The decision shows how difficult it can be for technology companies to gather enough data for AI development. Companies need large amounts of data to train AI systems, but finding that data in an ethical way is not always easy. This story matters because more and more companies are looking at their own workers as a source of AI training data. If employees do not feel safe or respected at work, this can damage trust between companies and their staff. It also shows that public pressure and privacy fears can influence big technology companies to change their plans quickly.

articles.questionB1: Do you think it is ever ethical for a company to track how its employees use their computers at work? Why or why not?
articles.summaryB2:
Meta has abruptly suspended a programme, launched just two months prior, that involved monitoring employees' computer usage with the stated aim of harvesting data for artificial intelligence training. The move came in response to mounting privacy fears among workers and advocacy groups, highlighting the acute tensions that arise when corporations attempt to repurpose internal data for AI development.

The episode exposes a dilemma at the heart of the AI industry. Technology firms require vast datasets to refine their models, yet sourcing that data responsibly has become an increasingly contentious issue. By turning to its own workforce as a data source, Meta appeared to be seeking a convenient alternative to publicly available content, which has itself come under intense legal scrutiny in recent years.

Critics argued that surveillance of this nature represented an overreach, particularly given the inherent power imbalance between an employer and its employees. Workers may feel unable to withhold consent freely when their jobs are at stake, calling into question whether any agreement obtained in such a context can be considered genuinely voluntary.

Meta's decision to discontinue the programme suggests that even one of the world's most powerful technology companies can be compelled to reverse course when faced with credible reputational risk. The incident serves as a cautionary tale for the broader tech sector: the drive to feed AI systems with data must be balanced against transparent, accountable practices that respect individual rights. Whether Meta will seek alternative data sources to fill this gap remains to be seen.

articles.title: It's not just about nudity warns actress - the complex reality of images and online abuse
articles.summaryB1: A new report says that tech companies and governments are not doing enough to protect women from online abuse. The report was written by an organisation called Chayn, which works to help women who have been harmed by technology. An actress also spoke about this problem and warned that people do not fully understand how serious it is. The report says that when someone shares a private image of another person without their permission, this is a form of abuse. However, many platforms and police focus only on whether the image shows nudity. This means that many harmful images — for example, photos that were shared to scare or control someone — are ignored because they do not contain nudity. The report says this is the wrong approach. What really matters is consent — whether the person agreed to have their image shared. Women often feel that they cannot get help because the law and tech companies do not see the full picture. This type of abuse can cause serious mental health problems and can destroy a person's life. The report calls on companies and authorities to change the way they think about these cases. They should look at the harm caused, not just whether the content is sexual. This is a growing problem that affects many women online.

vocabularyB1.definition: When someone officially allows you to do something

articles.questionB1: Do you think tech platforms and authorities have a responsibility to protect people from online abuse, even when nudity is not involved? Why?
articles.summaryB2: A report by the charity Chayn, supported by testimony from a prominent actress, has criticised tech companies and law enforcement for their narrow handling of image-based online abuse. The central argument is that by concentrating almost exclusively on nudity, both digital platforms and legal systems systematically overlook a wide range of harmful behaviour that does not involve explicit content. According to the report, this misguided focus fails to account for the real damage caused when private images are shared without consent — regardless of whether those images are sexual in nature. Many women find that their complaints are dismissed because the images in question do not meet a technical threshold of indecency, even when the intent behind sharing them was clearly to intimidate, control, or humiliate. This represents a fundamental misunderstanding of what constitutes abuse in a digital context. Chayn argues that the legal and technological frameworks currently in place are not fit for purpose, as they were largely designed around content moderation rather than victim protection. The report calls for a shift in how cases are assessed — placing consent and demonstrable harm at the centre of any evaluation, rather than the nature of the content itself. The actress involved emphasised that the psychological toll on victims is severe and long-lasting, and that without systemic reform, vulnerable women will continue to be let down by the very institutions meant to safeguard them.

articles.questionB2: Given that current frameworks prioritise content type over demonstrable harm, what systemic reform would most effectively shift the focus toward consent and victim protection in cases of online abuse?

articles.title: A super El Niño threatens disaster. Trump is handling it recklessly | Terry Garcia
articles.summaryB1: El Niño is a natural weather event that happens in the Pacific Ocean and causes extreme weather around the world. Scientists are now warning that a very powerful El Niño may be coming soon. In the past, El Niño events caused terrible disasters. In 1877, one of the strongest El Niños ever recorded led to severe drought across India, China, Africa, and Brazil. Harvests failed, and between 30 and 60 million people died in what became known as the Great Famine. That was about 3% of the world's population at the time. Today, we have much better tools to prepare for such events. Scientists use ocean monitoring systems to collect data and make forecasts. These advance warnings help governments act before disaster strikes, saving thousands of lives and billions of dollars every year. However, the article warns that the Trump administration has interrupted important data streams that scientists depend on for forecasting. The author, Terry Garcia, worked as a senior official at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. He says these monitoring systems must not be vulnerable to political decisions. If data collection is stopped for political reasons, our ability to anticipate dangerous weather events is seriously weakened. The main message is clear: protecting weather data systems should be treated as a matter of public safety, not politics.

vocabularyB1.definition: A long period with very little or no rain, causing water and food shortages
A prediction about what the weather or future events will be like
The regular watching and checking of something over a period of time
