articles.questionB1: Do you think governments should use weather forecasts and monitoring data to better prepare for natural disasters? Why or why not?
articles.summaryB2: A powerful El Niño event is building in the Pacific, and scientists warn it could trigger catastrophic weather disruptions worldwide. Writing in The Guardian, Terry Garcia — a former deputy administrator of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) — draws a stark historical parallel to illustrate what is at stake. In 1877, one of the most devastating El Niños on record coincided with widespread drought across Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Harvests collapsed, and between 30 and 60 million people perished in the so-called Great Famine — roughly 3% of the global population. Colonial policies compounded the suffering, but the underlying driver was the absence of any early warning system. What separates the modern world from those victims, Garcia argues, is not fortune but data. Sophisticated ocean monitoring networks now allow scientists to detect and track El Niño patterns months in advance, giving governments critical lead time to prepare emergency responses, protect food supplies, and evacuate at-risk populations. Yet Garcia warns that the Trump administration has recklessly interrupted the data streams underpinning these forecasts, exposing the entire early warning infrastructure to political interference. This, he contends, is a profound dereliction of duty. Weather monitoring systems that took decades to build should not be dismantled on a political whim. The implications are sobering: without reliable data, the capacity to anticipate and mitigate climate shocks diminishes sharply, potentially pushing vulnerable societies back toward the helplessness of the Victorian era.

To reduce the severity or harmful effects of something bad

articles.questionB2: To what extent does the deliberate interruption of scientific infrastructure for political reasons represent a dereliction of duty, and how might such decisions affect societies most exposed to climate shocks?

articles.title: Stop pretending EU's new border system is working, says airports chief

It is designed to scan the fingerprints and faces of travellers from outside the EU when they cross the border. However, the head of ACI Europe, which represents airports across Europe, is very worried about how the system will work in practice. He says the problems with EES are keeping him awake at night. He is especially concerned about what will happen during the busy summer travel season, when millions of people pass through European airports. The system has already been delayed many times, and airport leaders say they still do not have enough information or equipment to run it properly. Long queues at border checkpoints are expected, which could cause serious problems for passengers and airlines. The EU says the system will make borders more secure and help track people who stay in Europe longer than allowed. But airport officials say the plan is not ready. They want EU leaders to stop pretending that everything is fine and to admit that more time and preparation are needed before EES can be introduced successfully.

vocabularyB1.definition: The process of checking people and goods as they enter or leave a country
The unique patterns on the tips of your fingers, used to identify people
A line of people waiting for something
A place where people or vehicles are stopped and checked, for example at a border
Behaving as if something is true when it is not

articles.questionB1: Do you think airports can be ready for a new border control system without proper preparation? What problems could long queues cause for travellers?
articles.summaryB2: The head of ACI Europe, the lobbying body representing the continent's airports, has issued a blunt warning that the EU's Entry/Exit System — EES — is far from ready to be rolled out, and that the organisation can no longer afford to maintain the pretence that implementation is on track. EES is designed to replace passport stamping with biometric data collection, recording the fingerprints and facial images of all non-EU travellers at external borders. While the system's stated aim is to strengthen security and identify overstayers, repeated delays have left airports in a state of considerable uncertainty. With peak summer travel season approaching, the ACI Europe chief says the operational challenges are so severe that he cannot determine how airports will cope with the surge in passenger numbers. The concern is that mandatory biometric checks will create bottlenecks at border checkpoints, leading to prolonged queues and widespread disruption for airlines and travellers alike. Critics argue that the EU has consistently overstated its readiness to deploy the technology, leaving airport operators without adequate infrastructure, staffing guidance, or a coherent timeline. Supporters of EES counter that the long-term security benefits justify the short-term disruption. Nevertheless, industry figures are now calling on policymakers to acknowledge the gap between political ambition and operational reality, and to establish a more transparent and realistic schedule for the system's introduction.

vocabularyB2.definition: The act of behaving as if something is true when it clearly is not
Relating to the measurement of unique physical features, such as fingerprints or facial patterns, to identify people
Points in a process where movement slows down or stops because too many things are happening at once
Described something as better, bigger, or more advanced than it really is
Clear, logical, and well organised, so that all parts fit together sensibly

articles.questionB2: Given that the EU has apparently overstated its readiness to deploy EES, what responsibility do policymakers have to present a coherent and honest timeline to the aviation industry and the travelling public?

articles.title: Fuel sales halted in occupied Crimea as Ukraine targets oil facilities
articles.summaryB1: Ukraine has stopped fuel sales in Russian-occupied Crimea after attacking oil facilities there. This means people in Crimea cannot buy petrol or diesel at the moment. Before this, fuel had already been rationed, which means people could only buy a limited amount because there was not enough supply. Ukraine has been targeting the routes used to bring oil and other supplies into the areas that Russia controls. These attacks have made it very hard for Russia to keep fuel available for people living in occupied territories. Crimea is a peninsula that Russia took from Ukraine in 2014. Since Russia's full invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Crimea has become an important base for Russian military operations. Ukraine sees destroying fuel supplies as a way to weaken Russia's ability to fight. Without enough fuel, Russian forces and civilians in the region face serious difficulties. This situation shows how Ukraine is using targeted strikes on infrastructure to put pressure on Russia. For ordinary people living in Crimea, the shortage means long queues, limited travel, and daily life becoming much harder. The conflict is affecting not just soldiers, but also civilians who depend on fuel for heating, transport, and work.

vocabularyB1.definition: Limited to a fixed amount so that everyone gets a share during a shortage
Roads or paths used to bring goods like food or fuel to a place
Controlled by a foreign military force, not by the country it belongs to
Basic systems a society needs, like roads, power, and fuel networks
A piece of land almost completely surrounded by water, connected to the mainland

articles.questionB1: Why do you think Ukraine is targeting supply routes and fuel infrastructure in occupied territories — what effect might this have on the conflict?
articles.summaryB2: Ukraine has halted fuel sales across Russian-occupied Crimea following a series of strikes on oil facilities in the region. The move marks a further escalation in Kyiv's strategy of targeting energy and logistics infrastructure within Russian-controlled territories, aiming to degrade the operational capacity of occupying forces and complicate civilian life under Russian administration. Prior to the complete halt, fuel had already been rationed due to chronic shortages caused by repeated Ukrainian attacks on supply routes feeding the occupied zones. Crimea, annexed by Russia in 2014 in a move widely condemned by the international community, has served as a logistical hub for Russian military operations since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022. By severing the flow of fuel into the peninsula, Ukraine hopes to stretch Russian resources and slow military movements in the south. Critics of this approach point out that such strikes inevitably affect the civilian population, many of whom have little agency over the political situation they find themselves in. Supporters, however, argue that disrupting Russian supply chains is a legitimate and effective form of economic warfare. The fuel shortage adds to a pattern of mounting pressure on Russian-held territories, as Ukraine continues to exploit vulnerabilities in the occupier's logistical network. For residents of Crimea, the immediate reality is one of restricted mobility, economic strain, and deepening uncertainty.

vocabularyB2.definition: A situation becoming more serious, intense, or extreme than before
To reduce the effectiveness or strength of something, especially a military force
Taken over and made part of another country, usually by force
The ability of a person to make free choices and take independent action
Completely cutting off or ending a connection, supply, or relationship

articles.questionB2: To what extent is severing fuel supplies an effective and ethically justifiable strategy in modern conflict, given its inevitable impact on civilian agency and daily life?

articles.title: O'Leary extends Ryanair contract in deal that could net him over £130m
articles.summaryB1:
Michael O'Leary, the boss of Ryanair, has agreed to extend his contract with the airline until 2032. This means he will continue leading the company for several more years. O'Leary has been in charge of Ryanair for a very long time and is one of the most well-known figures in the aviation industry.

As part of the deal, O'Leary could earn a bonus of more than €150 million, which is around £130 million. This bonus depends on how well the airline performs during his contract period. If Ryanair meets certain targets, he will receive this large sum of money.

Ryanair is Europe's biggest low-cost carrier, and O'Leary is famous for keeping ticket prices very low. Under his leadership, the airline has grown enormously and now carries hundreds of millions of passengers every year.

Some people think that a bonus scheme of this size is too generous for one person. Others argue that a strong leader who delivers results deserves to be well rewarded. The airline's board of directors approved the deal, showing they believe O'Leary is worth the investment.

This news matters because it shows how airlines are trying to keep their top managers for longer periods. Stability at the top of a company can help it grow and plan for the future with more confidence.

vocabularyB1.definition: To make something last for a longer period of time than originally planned
Extra money paid to someone in addition to their normal salary, often as a reward
A company that transports passengers or goods, especially an airline
A plan or system organised to achieve a particular goal
A group of people responsible for making major decisions in a company

articles.questionB1: Do you think a bonus scheme worth over €150 million is fair for one airline boss? Why or why not?
articles.summaryB2:
Michael O'Leary, the long-serving chief executive of Ryanair, has secured a contract extension that will keep him at the helm of Europe's largest budget airline until 2032. The agreement includes a performance-linked remuneration package featuring a bonus that could net him in excess of €150 million — approximately £130 million — depending on how the airline fares over the coming years.

O'Leary's tenure at Ryanair spans decades, during which he transformed a small Irish airline into a dominant force in European aviation by relentlessly driving down costs and fares. His abrasive management style and outspoken personality have made him one of the most recognisable — and at times controversial — figures in the business world.

The sheer scale of the potential payout is likely to attract scrutiny from shareholder groups and the wider public, who may question whether any individual executive warrants such a substantial financial reward. Proponents, however, would argue that O'Leary's record of delivering growth and profitability justifies the terms of the deal. Ryanair's board clearly shares this view, having sanctioned the arrangement.

The extension also reflects a wider trend among major corporations of locking in experienced leadership amid uncertain economic conditions. For Ryanair, retaining O'Leary provides continuity at a time when the aviation sector faces ongoing pressures from rising fuel costs, environmental regulation, and intense competition. Whether the bonus targets will ultimately be met remains to be seen.

vocabularyB2.definition: The money and other benefits someone receives in exchange for their work
The period of time during which someone holds a particular job or position
Very careful and detailed examination or attention, often critical
Officially approved or permitted by an authority or organisation
The quality of staying consistent and uninterrupted over a period of time

articles.questionB2: Given the level of scrutiny that executive remuneration packages typically attract, do you think Ryanair's board made a wise decision in approving this deal? What factors should influence such choices?

articles.title: How the social media ban could reshape how all of us use the internet
articles.summaryB1: Australia has passed a new law that bans children under 16 from using social media. This is one of the strictest rules of its kind in the world. The law means that platforms like TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook must stop young people from making accounts. If these companies do not follow the rules, they can be fined very large amounts of money. The ban has started a big debate around the world. Some people support the idea because they want to protect young people from harmful content and online dangers. However, others are worried about the consequences of this decision. One concern is that young people use social media to learn new things and discover information. If they lose access to these platforms, they may miss out on knowledge that helps them grow. There is also a question about how the ban will be enforced in practice. Websites may need to check the age of all users, not just young people. This could change how everyone uses the internet, not only teenagers. Some experts believe that age verification systems could affect privacy for all users. The situation in Australia is being watched closely by governments in other countries, who may decide to introduce similar restrictions in the future.

vocabularyB1.definition: An official rule that stops people from doing something.
A website or app where people share content and communicate online.
The results or effects of an action or decision.
Made sure that a rule or law is followed by people.
Rules that limit what people are allowed to do.

articles.questionB1: Do you think a ban on social media for young people will have more positive or negative consequences for society? Why?
articles.summaryB2: Australia's decision to prohibit children under 16 from accessing social media has ignited a global conversation about the future of digital life — not just for young people, but for internet users of all ages. The legislation, among the most sweeping of its kind worldwide, places the burden of compliance squarely on tech companies such as Meta, TikTok, and Snapchat, which face substantial fines for failing to prevent underage users from creating accounts. Proponents of the law argue that shielding minors from harmful online content and predatory behaviour is long overdue. Critics, however, contend that the measure is disproportionate and risks depriving young people of a space where they seek information, build communities, and develop digital literacy at a formative stage of their lives. Perhaps the most far-reaching implication of the ban concerns age verification. In order to enforce the restrictions effectively, platforms may be compelled to introduce identity-checking systems for all users, fundamentally altering how people interact with the web. Privacy advocates warn that such systems could lead to widespread data collection, creating new vulnerabilities for adults and children alike. The Australian example is being scrutinised by policymakers across Europe and North America, many of whom are grappling with similar questions about how to regulate social media without inadvertently curtailing freedoms that have become central to modern life.

vocabularyB2.definition: Very wide in range or effect; affecting many things or people at once.
Following the rules or laws that have been set by an authority.
Too large or too small compared to what is fair or expected.
Weaknesses that make someone or something open to harm or attack.
Reducing or limiting something, especially a right or an activity.

articles.questionB2: Given the risk of curtailing digital freedoms through sweeping age verification systems, how should governments balance protecting young people online with preserving privacy rights for all users?

articles.title: ‘A sacred kind of sound’: inside a solar-powered journey to preserve the music of church organs
articles.summaryB1:
A Canadian musician named Michael Cloud Duguay has made a new album by recording pipe organs in old churches across Newfoundland, a large island in eastern Canada. Pipe organs are very old musical instruments that use air, pipes, and pedals to make powerful sounds. Many of these organs are now rare because small church communities cannot afford to maintain them.

Duguay and his team travelled to remote villages, including a small town called Aguathuna with only about 400 people. They used a mobile studio powered by solar energy, so they did not need electricity from the local grid. They recorded the organs in their natural setting, capturing every detail of their sound.

The album, called Kingdom Come, Kingdom Go, is a collection of quiet, thoughtful pieces of music. It also works as an audio documentary, meaning it tells a story through sound. Duguay wanted to preserve the music of these instruments before they disappear.

Pipe organs are special because they were built to fill large spaces with sound. People often describe the experience of hearing one as almost spiritual. By recording them in their original churches, Duguay has created both an artistic work and a historical record. This project shows how music can help us remember things that might otherwise be lost forever.

vocabularyB1.definition: Far away from cities or towns, difficult to reach
To keep something safe so it does not disappear or get damaged
A recording space that can move from place to place
Parts of a machine or instrument that you press with your foot
A group of people who regularly attend the same church

articles.questionB1: Why do you think it is important to preserve rare instruments like pipe organs, and what other things in your community might be worth recording?
articles.summaryB2:
Canadian composer Michael Cloud Duguay has released Kingdom Come, Kingdom Go, an album born from a week-long expedition across Newfoundland to document the pipe organs found in the island's ageing and often struggling rural churches. Armed with a solar-powered mobile studio, Duguay and his collaborators travelled to isolated communities — including Aguathuna, a windswept settlement of barely 400 residents on a craggy peninsula — where they recorded instruments ranging from the modest to the monumental.

Pipe organs are among the most architecturally complex of all musical instruments, relying on intricate systems of keys, stops, bellows, reeds, and foot pedals to generate sound on a scale that has historically been described as approximating the divine. Yet many of these instruments face an uncertain future, as declining congregations in rural areas find it harder to maintain them.

Duguay's project sits at the intersection of artistic creation and cultural preservation. The resulting album is elegiac in tone — a word that captures its mood of quiet mourning for something fading — and functions simultaneously as a composed work and an audio documentary. By collaging field recordings with original composition, Duguay resists straightforward nostalgia, instead creating something that acknowledges loss without surrendering to it.

The project also raises questions about who bears responsibility for safeguarding endangered cultural heritage, particularly in communities that lack the resources to do so themselves.

vocabularyB2.definition: Having a sad, reflective quality, mourning something lost or passing away
Combining different recorded or found materials together to create a new work
An organised journey made for a specific purpose, often to a remote place
Protecting something important from harm, loss, or disappearance
Cut off from other places or people; remote and hard to reach

articles.questionB2: In what ways does Duguay's decision to use collaging rather than straightforward composition challenge our assumptions about what it means to safeguard endangered cultural heritage through art?

articles.title: From mobile jungles to shadow art: how Dutch people try to beat the heat
articles.summaryB1:
The Netherlands is experiencing very hot summers, and many Dutch people are struggling to stay cool. Most homes in the country were built for cold, wet weather, so they are not designed to handle extreme heat. Now, a national heatwave plan has been activated to help people manage the situation.

One simple but effective tip has gone viral on social media. Eline Coolen, who works as a heat coordinator at Amsterdam's public health institute, shared advice about how to block the sun. She urged people to hang curtains or sheets outside their windows, not inside. This stops the sun's rays from entering the home before they even reach the glass. You can use temporary rails or just drape the fabric over the outside of the window.

This idea spread quickly online because it is so easy and cheap to do. Many Amsterdam residents have large windows, which let in a lot of sunlight and heat.

Health experts are encouraging households to try these simple hacks to stay cool. The situation shows how climate change is forcing people in traditionally cool countries to adapt their daily habits. What works in southern Europe may now be needed in the north too. Small changes at home can make a real difference during a heatwave.

vocabularyB1.definition: A period of unusually hot weather that lasts for several days
Started or put into action, especially an official plan or system
To strongly encourage or advise someone to do something
To hang or place cloth loosely over something
Clever, simple tricks or tips that solve everyday problems easily

articles.questionB1: What simple hacks could you use at home to stay cool during a heatwave, and why do you think such tips spread so quickly online?
articles.summaryB2:
As the Netherlands grapples with increasingly intense summers, authorities have activated a national heatwave plan to protect public health — a response that highlights a growing mismatch between the country's housing stock and its changing climate. Dutch homes, historically designed for damp, cold northern European conditions, are poorly equipped to cope with prolonged heat, leaving residents vulnerable and searching for solutions.

Among the most widely shared remedies is a deceptively simple one: hanging curtains or sheets on the outside of windows rather than the inside. Eline Coolen, Amsterdam's heat coordinator at the city's public health institute, posted the advice on social media, where it quickly went viral. By positioning fabric externally, residents can intercept the sun's rays before they penetrate the glass, preventing heat from building up indoors in the first place. Temporary curtain rails or loosely draped sheets are all that is needed.

The tip resonated strongly with city-dwellers, many of whom live in homes with large windows that amplify solar gain. Its rapid spread reflects both the ingenuity of low-cost adaptation and the public's appetite for accessible, practical guidance during extreme weather events.

The episode points to a wider challenge facing temperate-climate nations: as heatwaves become more frequent and severe, societies built around cold-weather assumptions must adapt their infrastructure and everyday behaviour. Whether through grassroots improvisation or coordinated public health campaigns, northern Europe is being forced to reimagine what it means to live comfortably through summer.

vocabularyB2.definition: Struggles to deal with a difficult problem or situation
A situation where two things do not fit or work well together
To stop or catch something before it reaches its destination
To make something stronger, louder, or more intense
The ability to find clever, creative solutions to problems

articles.questionB2: To what extent does the viral spread of low-cost advice like external curtains reflect a failure of infrastructure planning, and what does this mismatch reveal about how societies respond to climate adaptation?

articles.title: Half of France under red heat alert as alcohol banned at street music festival
articles.summaryB1: France is experiencing a very serious heatwave. The government has placed half of the country under a red heat alert, which is the highest level of warning. This means that temperatures are extremely dangerous and people need to take care. Authorities say that temperatures could reach historic highs on Monday, matching the hottest days ever recorded in France. A red alert tells people to stay indoors, drink water often, and avoid going outside during the hottest parts of the day. The elderly, young children, and people with health problems are especially at risk. At the same time, a large street music festival is taking place in France. Because of the extreme heat, authorities have decided to ban alcohol at the festival. This decision was made to protect people who are dancing and spending time outside in the sun. Drinking alcohol in hot weather can make the body lose water faster and increase the risk of heatstroke. France has suffered from deadly heatwaves before, most notably in 2003, when thousands of people died. Events like this remind us that extreme heat is a real danger to public health. Governments must act quickly and clearly to warn people and keep them safe during such weather conditions.

vocabularyB1.definition: A long period of unusually hot weather that can be dangerous
An official warning that tells people about a serious danger
People or organisations with official power to make decisions and rules
An official rule that stops people from doing something
A dangerous medical condition caused by the body getting too hot

articles.questionB1: When authorities issue a red alert during a heatwave, who do you think is most at risk and why?
articles.summaryB2: France is grappling with a severe heatwave that has prompted the government to place approximately half the country under a red heat alert — the most extreme tier in the national warning system. Forecasters predict that temperatures will peak on Monday, potentially rivalling the all-time records set during France's catastrophic 2003 heatwave, in which an estimated 15,000 people perished. The red alert designation obliges local authorities to mobilise emergency services, open cooling centres, and conduct welfare checks on vulnerable populations, including the elderly and those with chronic illnesses. Simultaneously, the heatwave has forced organisers of a major street music festival to impose a sweeping prohibition on alcohol consumption at the event. Public health officials argued that alcohol accelerates dehydration, dramatically compounding the physiological strain already placed on the body by extreme heat, and that permitting its sale could expose attendees to life-threatening conditions. The convergence of a mass outdoor gathering and record-breaking temperatures has highlighted the tension between cultural traditions and public safety imperatives. Critics of the ban have questioned whether outright prohibition is proportionate, while health experts maintain it is a necessary precaution. The episode reflects a wider pattern across Europe, where policymakers are being compelled to reassess how public events are managed as episodes of extreme heat become more frequent and more intense.

vocabularyB2.definition: Struggling to deal with a difficult or serious problem
An official order that completely forbids something by law or authority
A harmful condition in which the body loses too much water
Making an already bad situation worse by adding more problems
Appropriate in size or degree relative to the situation; not excessive

articles.questionB2: To what extent do you think imposing a prohibition on alcohol at a public festival is a proportionate response to extreme heat, and where should the line between personal freedom and public safety be drawn?

articles.title: Is Germany looking again at coal-powered electricity?
articles.summaryB1: Germany is one of the biggest users of coal in Europe. For many years, the country burned coal to make electricity. Coal is a fossil fuel that produces a lot of carbon dioxide, which is bad for the climate. Because of this, Germany made a plan to stop using coal completely by 2038. However, this plan may now change. The reason is that natural gas has become very expensive. Germany used to buy a lot of gas from Russia, but after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, Germany stopped buying Russian gas. This made gas prices go up sharply. Now, some people in Germany think it may be cheaper to use coal again instead of gas to generate electricity. Coal is easier to find and costs less right now. But environmental groups are not happy about this idea. They say burning more coal will release more pollution into the air and make climate change worse. Germany is trying to balance two things: keeping energy affordable for people and companies, and also protecting the environment. The German government has not made a final decision yet. This situation shows how difficult energy policy can be, especially when countries depend on fuel from other nations. Many Europeans are watching to see what Germany will decide to do about its energy supply.

vocabularyB1.definition: A natural energy source like coal, oil, or gas formed from ancient living things underground.
To produce or create something, for example electricity.
To let something out into the environment, such as gas or smoke.
Not too expensive; something that most people have enough money to pay for.
To need something or someone and not be able to manage without them.

articles.questionB1: Do you think it is ever acceptable for a country to use fossil fuels if they help keep energy affordable? Why or why not?
articles.summaryB2: Germany, long regarded as a leader in the energy transition away from carbon-intensive fuels, is now reconsidering its commitment to phasing out coal-powered electricity. The country had previously set a target to abandon coal entirely by 2038, a pledge driven by ambitious climate goals and public pressure from environmental advocates. However, the dramatic surge in natural gas prices has forced policymakers to reassess their priorities. Germany's heavy reliance on Russian gas prior to the invasion of Ukraine in 2022 left the country exposed when it severed those energy ties. The resulting supply shortfall sent gas prices soaring and pushed some industry voices to argue that coal offers a more economical and readily available alternative in the short term. Critics, however, warn that any reversal would be a serious setback for Germany's climate commitments and could undermine the credibility of European decarbonisation efforts more broadly. Environmental organisations point out that coal emits significantly more carbon dioxide per unit of energy than gas, meaning even a temporary revival would have measurable consequences for emissions targets. The German government finds itself caught between the economic realities facing households and businesses and the long-term obligations it has made to reduce carbon output. No definitive policy shift has been announced, but the debate illustrates the tension inherent in transitioning away from fossil fuels when energy security remains precarious.

vocabularyB2.definition: Gradually stopping the use of something over a period of time.
To look at a situation again carefully and possibly change your opinion or plan.
An event that slows progress or makes a situation worse than before.
The process of reducing or eliminating carbon dioxide emissions from energy and industry.
Uncertain and potentially dangerous; not stable or secure.

articles.questionB2: To what extent does Germany's possible reversal on phasing out coal reveal a fundamental tension between short-term energy security and long-term decarbonisation commitments in European policy?

articles.title: New video game console aims to get kids moving
articles.summaryB1: A new video game console called the Nex Playground has been designed to make children more active while they play. Unlike traditional gaming systems, this device encourages kids to move their bodies instead of just sitting on a sofa. The console uses special technology to track players' movements, turning physical activity into part of the gameplay. Parents who are worried about their children spending too much time in front of screens may find this product appealing. The Nex Playground will go on sale on 22 June in the UK and Ireland. It will cost £269, which is around €319. This price puts it in competition with other popular gaming systems already on the market. The idea of combining exercise with video games is not completely new, but this console aims to make it more accessible and fun for younger players. Health experts often warn that children today do not get enough physical activity, so a product like this could help address that problem. Whether parents decide to purchase the device will likely depend on how entertaining the games actually are. If children enjoy the experience, it could become a popular choice for families looking for a way to get their kids off the sofa and moving around.

vocabularyB1.definition: Moving your body and doing physical things rather than staying still
To follow or record someone's movements using technology
Attractive or interesting; making you want to have or try something
Easy for people to use, reach, or understand
To buy something, especially something that costs a lot of money

articles.questionB1: Do you think video games that keep children active are more appealing than traditional games, and why?
articles.summaryB2: A new gaming console called the Nex Playground is set to launch on 22 June in the UK and Ireland, priced at £269 (€319), with the explicit goal of combating childhood inactivity by integrating physical movement into gameplay. The device uses motion-tracking technology to detect players' body movements, effectively transforming the living room into a space for exercise rather than passive entertainment. The product enters a market already familiar with movement-based gaming — Nintendo's Wii console pioneered the concept nearly two decades ago — yet the Nex Playground appears to be positioning itself as a contemporary alternative tailored specifically for younger audiences. From a public health standpoint, the timing is noteworthy. Childhood obesity and sedentary behaviour remain persistent concerns across the UK, and advocates for children's wellbeing have long called for innovative solutions that make physical activity more enticing to screen-reliant generations. Whether a £269 price point proves to be a deterrent for many families remains an open question, particularly given the cost-of-living pressures currently affecting British households. Critics might also question whether the novelty of movement-based play can sustain children's engagement over time, or whether the initial enthusiasm will wane as it did for many Wii owners. Nonetheless, the Nex Playground represents a genuine attempt to reconcile the undeniable pull of digital entertainment with the growing imperative to keep children physically engaged.

vocabularyB2.definition: Actively working to stop or reduce something harmful or negative
Describing a lifestyle involving too much sitting and very little physical movement
Something that discourages people from doing or buying something
To gradually become weaker, smaller, or less enthusiastic over time
To find a way to make two opposing things exist or work together

articles.questionB2: Given that enthusiasm for movement-based gaming has historically been known to wane, what would need to be true for the Nex Playground to succeed where previous consoles struggled to maintain long-term engagement?

articles.title: ‘The beauty of the useless’: Spain’s super-thin restaurant napkins are throwaway art treasures
articles.summaryB1:
In Spain, bars and restaurants have small metal containers on tables filled with very thin paper napkins called servilletas. These napkins are famous for being almost completely useless. They do not soak up liquids well, and they are too weak to blow your nose with. If you try to clean greasy fingers with one, you usually need five or six of them just to get the job done. Their texture is very papery and thin, which makes them poor at their main purpose.

Despite being so ineffective, these flimsy napkins have survived for many years without changing. In a world where everything is being made faster, smarter, and more efficient, the Spanish servilleta has stayed exactly the same. This makes them unusual and, according to some people, charming.

A new photo book now celebrates these throwaway items as cultural treasures. The book recognises that the napkins represent something special about Spanish food culture and daily life. They are small, disposable objects, but they carry a certain identity that many people find appealing.

The story of these napkins is a reminder that not everything needs to be optimised or improved. Sometimes an object becomes beloved precisely because it is imperfect. The servilleta is a tiny piece of throwaway art that millions of people use every day without thinking much about it.

vocabularyB1.definition: Thin, weak, and not strong enough for its purpose
The way a surface feels when you touch it
Made to be used once and then thrown away
Attractive or interesting to people
Improved to work as well and efficiently as possible

articles.questionB1: Do you think a disposable everyday object can become a cultural treasure? What makes something appealing enough to celebrate?
articles.summaryB2:
A new photo book has turned its lens on one of Spain's most overlooked everyday objects: the servilleta, a wafer-thin paper napkin found in the ubiquitous small metal dispensers on bar and restaurant tables across the Iberian peninsula. The book makes a compelling case for recognising these throwaway items as miniature cultural artefacts, despite — or perhaps because of — their near-total functional inadequacy.

Anyone who has eaten tapas in Spain will be well acquainted with the servilleta's shortcomings. The napkins are essentially impermeable to liquid, making them useless for mopping up spills. They are too fragile to survive contact with a runny nose, and so ineffective at cleaning oily fingers that diners routinely go through half a dozen per croqueta. Yet these very flaws appear to be the source of their enduring charm.

What makes the servilleta culturally intriguing is its stubborn resistance to the relentless optimisation that defines modern consumer culture. In an era when products are constantly redesigned for efficiency and performance, this particular item has remained defiantly unchanged, retaining its papery texture and its cheerful uselessness.

The photo book reframes this apparent failure as a form of quiet defiance — an accidental monument to imperfection in an age obsessed with utility. By elevating the servilleta to the status of art object, the project invites us to reconsider what we value in everyday life and why some things are worth preserving precisely because they refuse to be improved.

vocabularyB2.definition: Found or seen everywhere, very common
The state of not being good enough or capable enough
In a way that openly resists or refuses to obey expectations
Presents something in a new or different way to change how it is understood
The practical usefulness of something

articles.questionB2: The photo book reframes the servilleta's inadequacy as cultural value. To what extent can the deliberate preservation of imperfect, inefficient objects serve as meaningful resistance to modern consumer culture?

articles.title: France cancels events and restricts alcohol consumption amid brutal heatwave
articles.summaryB1: France is experiencing a very dangerous heatwave, with temperatures expected to reach 42 degrees Celsius in some areas. Because of this extreme heat, French authorities have taken serious steps to protect people. More than a third of the country has been placed under a red heat alert, which means there is a danger to life. In total, about 53 million people — more than 75% of France's population — are living under some level of heat warning. Authorities have cancelled some outdoor sports events because the heat could be harmful to both athletes and spectators. They have also restricted alcohol consumption at the Fête de la Musique, a popular nationwide music festival held every year on 21st June. Alcohol is banned or limited at this event because drinking in extreme heat can make people more ill. A record 35 of France's 96 mainland departments are on the highest alert level. Another 45 departments are under an orange warning. Heatwaves like this are becoming more common in Europe due to climate change. Events like this show how governments must act quickly to keep people safe. When temperatures rise so high, everyday activities become dangerous, and public health becomes the top priority.

vocabularyB1.definition: A long period of unusually hot weather that can be dangerous
People or organisations with official power to make decisions and rules
Officially limited or controlled, so something cannot be done freely
An official warning that tells people about a possible danger
The act of eating, drinking, or using something

articles.questionB1: When authorities issue a heat alert and restrict certain activities, do you think people always follow the rules, and why?
articles.summaryB2: France is grappling with one of its most severe heatwaves on record, with temperatures forecast to exceed 40 degrees Celsius across large parts of the country from Monday, peaking at 42C in the worst-affected regions. In response, French authorities have placed a record 35 of the country's 96 mainland departments under a red heat alert — the highest danger-to-life designation — while a further 45 departments remain under orange warnings. Altogether, some 53 million people, representing just over 75% of the population, are subject to at least a level one or two heat advisory. The scale of the authorities' intervention has been sweeping. Several outdoor sporting events have been cancelled outright, and alcohol consumption has been curtailed at the Fête de la Musique, France's beloved annual nationwide music festival traditionally held on 21st June. The decision to impose restrictions on alcohol at such a culturally embedded event reflects the gravity of the situation; heat and alcohol together dramatically accelerate the risk of dehydration and heatstroke. This episode highlights a growing challenge for European governments: how to balance public safety with cultural and economic life during extreme weather events. Scientists have long warned that climate change will make such heatwaves both more frequent and more intense, placing mounting pressure on public health infrastructure and emergency response systems across the continent.

vocabularyB2.definition: Struggling to deal with a difficult or serious problem
An official label or category given to something by an authority
Reduced or stopped, especially by official order or necessity
Deeply established as part of a society's traditions and way of life
To make something happen faster or increase in speed or intensity

articles.questionB2: Given that the Fête de la Musique is a culturally embedded national tradition, how should governments decide when public safety measures justify curtailed freedoms during extreme weather events?

articles.title: Meloni tells Trump to 'focus on your own popularity' as row escalates
articles.summaryB1: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and US President Donald Trump are having a public argument. Trump suggested that Meloni 'begged' him for a photo at the G7 summit, a meeting of leaders from seven powerful countries. He also questioned whether she was still popular with Italian voters. Meloni responded quickly and sharply. She told Trump to 'focus on your own popularity' instead of commenting on hers. This shows that the two leaders, who were once seen as political allies, now have a tense relationship. Meloni leads a right-wing government in Italy and has generally supported good relations with the United States. However, Trump's words were seen as disrespectful by many people. A summit is a formal meeting between world leaders, usually to discuss big global issues. When Trump questioned her popularity, Meloni did not stay quiet. She fired back in a confident and direct way. This kind of public dispute between close allies is unusual and has surprised many political observers. It matters because Italy and the United States are both members of NATO and important partners. When their leaders argue publicly, it can affect how the two countries work together in the future.

vocabularyB1.definition: Countries or people who support each other and work together toward common goals
A formal meeting between leaders of different countries to discuss important issues
A serious argument or disagreement between two people or groups
Feeling nervous, uncomfortable, or unfriendly, often before or during a conflict
People who watch and pay attention to events, especially in politics or society

articles.questionB1: When allies have a public dispute like this, do you think it helps or hurts their countries' relationship? Why?
articles.summaryB2: A diplomatic spat between Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and US President Donald Trump has escalated into a full public exchange of barbs, raising eyebrows among political commentators on both sides of the Atlantic. Trump ignited the row by suggesting that Meloni had 'begged' him for a photograph at the recent G7 summit, while simultaneously casting doubt on her standing with Italian voters — a pointed jab at her political credibility. Meloni, who leads Italy's right-wing government and has cultivated a carefully managed relationship with Trump since his return to the White House, responded with characteristic bluntness, telling the US president to 'focus on your own popularity' rather than speculate about hers. The exchange is notable for several reasons. Meloni has long been regarded as one of Europe's leaders most ideologically aligned with Trump's brand of nationalism, making the friction between them all the more striking. Her willingness to publicly rebuke him suggests she is unwilling to allow perceived slights to go unanswered, even at the cost of straining a relationship she has worked to maintain. The incident also highlights the unpredictable nature of Trump's interpersonal diplomacy, in which personal remarks can quickly overshadow formal alliances. As Italy and the United States remain partners within NATO, the repercussions of this very public falling-out remain to be seen.

vocabularyB2.definition: A short, petty argument or disagreement, often between people who usually get along
Sharp, hurtful remarks intended to criticise or mock someone
To criticise or speak sharply to someone because of something wrong they said or did
Small insults or acts that show disrespect or a lack of regard for someone
Negative consequences or effects that follow an action or event, often felt later

articles.questionB2: Given the repercussions that public spats between allied leaders can have on international cooperation, do you think Meloni's decision to respond so openly was wise or politically risky?

articles.title: Brexit cost 6% of UK economy, Bank of England company data suggests
articles.summaryB1: A new study from the Bank of England suggests that Brexit has cost the UK economy about 6% of its total output. This means the UK economy is now much smaller than it would have been if Britain had stayed in the European Union. Researchers looked at data from thousands of companies to reach this conclusion. They compared how UK businesses performed after Brexit with how similar businesses in other countries grew during the same period. The results show a clear gap between the two. Before Brexit, UK companies were growing at a similar rate to companies in other countries. After Brexit, UK company growth slowed down significantly. The study also found that trade between the UK and EU fell after Britain left the single market. This affected many sectors, including manufacturing and retail. Some people disagree with these findings. They argue that other factors, such as the COVID-19 pandemic and global inflation, also damaged the economy. However, the researchers tried to separate these effects in their analysis. For Polish people watching from Europe, this story is a reminder of how major political decisions can have long-term economic consequences. The debate about whether Brexit was the right choice continues in Britain today.

vocabularyB1.definition: The total amount of goods or services a country or company produces
A trading area where countries share the same rules and goods move freely
The process of making products in factories on a large scale
A general rise in prices that makes money worth less over time
The results or effects that happen because of a decision or action

articles.questionB1: What do you think are the most serious consequences of a country leaving a single market like the EU?
articles.summaryB2: New analysis based on Bank of England company-level data indicates that Brexit has reduced UK economic output by approximately 6%, painting a sobering picture of the long-term cost of Britain's departure from the European Union. The research compares the performance of UK firms against counterparts in comparable economies, establishing a clear divergence that emerged after the UK left the EU's single market and customs union. Prior to Brexit, British companies tracked closely with their international peers in terms of growth and productivity. Afterwards, a persistent gap opened up, suggesting that reduced access to EU markets has acted as a structural drag on the economy. Trade volumes between the UK and the EU dropped noticeably following the transition, particularly affecting sectors dependent on frictionless cross-border supply chains, such as manufacturing and food production. Critics of the findings caution against attributing all of the UK's economic underperformance solely to Brexit. They point out that the COVID-19 pandemic and the global inflationary shock of 2022 also weighed heavily on growth during the same period. Researchers, however, attempted to isolate Brexit's specific impact by controlling for these external variables. The study adds to a growing body of evidence suggesting that the economic costs of Brexit are real and enduring, though the political debate in Britain over the decision remains deeply polarised.

vocabularyB2.definition: A situation where two things that were similar start moving in different directions
A long-term, built-in factor that slows economic growth continuously
Describing trade or movement that happens without barriers, delays or extra costs
To separate one specific cause or factor from other influences in an analysis
Divided into two strongly opposing groups with little agreement between them

articles.questionB2: Given that researchers attempted to isolate Brexit's impact from other factors like the pandemic, how confident can we be that the observed economic divergence is primarily caused by Brexit itself?
